Hr.	LEMIEUX-by Mr. Bickerdikeasked :
1.	Has the Minister of Marine and Fisheries received the following petition :-
To the Honourable Raymond Prefontaine, Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
The petition of the undersigned fish merchants, fishermen and others interested in the fishing industry in the district of Gaspe, respectfully showeth
That the fisheries of the Gulf of St. Lawrence are seriously injured by the use of trap-nets for codfish and herring which have been proved to be very destructive to the fisheries, owing to the fact that large and small fish are indiscriminately caught ; the claim that the large mesh gives freedom of way to small fish is not justified by experience, it being conclusively proved that the large fish block up the meshes, and the small fish, when in the trap, are unable to escape.
That the seining of herring, caplin and any other fish in the spring of the year and at all times for the purpose of fertilizing lands, is a wanton waste of valuable product, and a great detriment to the profitable prosecution of the fisheries, and should be discouraged by every possible means, in order that those fish may be used solely for the purposes of food and bait ; otherwise our cod-fishing industry will be ruined, as no bait can be procured. Your petitioners also pray that the trapping of all kinds of fish by means of steam trawling be made contrary to law.
Wherefore, your petitioners urgently request that you will be pleased to take the necessary measures to prohibit the use of trap-nets for codfish and herring, and also prohibit the use of herring, caplin and other fish for fertilizing purposes. And your petitioners, as duty bound, will ever pray.

2.	What action does the Department of Marine and Fisheries intend to take on this question ?
The MINISTER OB' MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine) :
1.	Yes, through Mr. Lemieux, M.P.
2.	The department, after fully considering the matter, has reached the conclusion that sufficient grounds do not exist for taking action on the lines of the petition.
The department does not feel justified in taking an action in the matter, as the three principal statements in the petition are not justified by the facts as officially reported.
The petitioners claim that codfish and herring have injured the fisheries of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Statistics officially published show that the cod and herring fishery during the past few years, has shown no decrease in productiveness. In fact, these fish have been unusually abundant, and any local decrease is accounted for by merely local circumstances-rough weather, &c.
The petitioners protest against the seining of herring, caplin and other fish in the spring to be used for fertilizing purposes. While the Fisheries Act prohibits the catching of fish for use as manure, the department has not felt justified in strenuously enforcing the law in this respect, as such fish as herring in the spring are in poor condition, and frequently not very marketable. Such fish as are not marketable, instead of being wasted are used on the land. To this the department sees no objection.
Tlie petitioners protest against the use of steam trawls. This allegation is not found to have a very good basis according to the reports of the departmental officers. Steam trawling is so limited at present that special restrictive steps would not be justifiable.

speechtext: 1. Did the Minister of Public Works receive the following complaint against Captain W. 8. Larkin, of the steam dredge 'Prince Edward'?

Tarte,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I have been employed on the dredge ' Prince Edward,' as a deck hand, for the past five years. The dredge is under the control of Captain W. S. Larkin, of Alberton, in this province. In common with some of the rest of the crew, I have to complain of Captain Larkin's conduct, which is objectionable on the following grounds :-
1.	There has frequently been drinking and disorder on board, and the .captain himself has often given evidence of over-drinking, and sometimes his conduct was violent.
2.	His language was frequently blasphemous and indecent, and he often offended the religious convictions of some of the men on board.
For the reasons above mentioned, and for others with which I will not trouble you at present, life on board the dredge became so unpleasant that, though I am a poor man, I could not endure it further under the same conditions. I can put up with much, but not with further service tinder Captain Larkin. If he is allowed to continue in his present position, it will be a great injury to the Liberal party, of which I and my friends have long been supporters, and will have the effect of turning away more of those who object to having men of Captain Larkin's stamp, in places of authority.
I am respectfully yours, &e.,

House in Committee of Supply.
Public works-chargeable to income-miscellaneous-to cover balance of expenditures of works already authorized for which the appropriations may be insufficient, provided that amount for each work does not exceed $100, $3,000.
['There seems to be some misunderstanding about this Bill, Mr. Chairman. I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.']

I understand, Mr. Chairman, that under the item which you have just brought to the notice of the committee, we are entitled to discuss the general principle of some of the preceding items. I have not been fortunate enough to be present when some of the items regarding the provipce of Quebec came under the notice of the committee, and I desire now to obtain from the government, if possible, a declaration which,
I think we are quite entitled to in respect of the control of these large expenditures which we have voted and are still busy voting in connection with harbours and rivers. If ever a Committee of Supply of this House was entitled to such a declaration we are entitled to it now-and I will briefly as possible explain to the House upon what I rest that proposition. When the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. PrSfontaine) came for re-election in the district in Montreal, in the division of Maisonneuve, he came at a time when there had been grave discussions in the province of Quebec, and more particularly in the districts of Montreal, and, perhaps, more especially in the division where he sought re-election, in regard to what was deemed at that time a shuffle of portfolios in the present cabinet. It is known to every member of this House that, after the resignation or dismissal of the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) grave difficulties arose as to who should replace that gentleman in the cabinet of the right hon. the Premier (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). It is known to us particularly in the province of Quebec that very grave difficulties arose among the members of the party in the city of Montreal as to the claims of certain parties to the portfolio which had been left vacant. After a considerable space of time, pressure was brought to bear upon the right hon. the Premier in this direction- that the portfolio should not be given to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prfifontaine). Reasons were urged right and left. We heard some of these reasons on the street. But they were urged even in the government organs of Montreal. Two newspapers which support the government and receive support from the government, one to a very considerable extent, publicly, a day or two-yes, I believe even twelve hours-before my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was called to his present office, urged strongly and publicly that it was not right, for the reasons stated in these newspapers, that my hon. friend should succeed purely and simply to the estate left vacant at the head of that important department. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will remember in what scathing terms the Montreal 1 Witness claiming, as it has always claimed, that it was a supporter of the present government, urged upon the government and on all serious men of the party which support that government, that my hon. friend should not be given that portfolio, should not even enter the cabinet of the right hon. gentleman. Another organ, the official organ of the government in the city of Montreal, the Montreal ' Herald,' in a very strong article, a very few hours, as I have said, before my right hon. friend had fixed his choice upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, actually warned the government against the

choice of my hon. friend and gave reasons therefor, with which reasons I shall presently make the members of the committee acquainted. X mention these facts in order to show that members of my right hon. friend's party in Montreal, even more than the members of the party to which I have the honour to belong, were eager, were anxious, and publicly expressed that anxiety, that my hon. friend should not be nominated to the portfolio of Public Works. The article of the Montreal ' Herald ' created a great sensation, not only in political circles, but all over the city of Montreal, and throughout the province of Quebec. And these are the terms, calm, moderate, but forceful, in which the Montreal ' Herald ' reviewed the situation but a few hours before that important nomination was made. I believe in that same number of the Montreal ' Herald ' of the 10th of November, the announcement was made that my hon. friend had been officially chosen, and that his partisans had succeeded after a very severe struggle. It is entitled 1 Cabinet changes.'
The announcement is made that Sir Wilfrid Laurier has asked Hon. James Sutherland, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to take the portfolio of Public Works, and has offered Mr. Sutherland's portfolio to Mr. Raymond Prefon-taine, M.P., for Maisoneuve and Terrebonne. The translation of Mr. Sutherland from the one department to the other will be viewed with favour in Ontario, in which province it had been a standing complaint that the great spending departments of the government were in the hands of representatives of other and smaller provinces. The complaint has not been without reason, for Ontario is the largest contributor to the country's revenue. No doubt the consideration of this fact had its influence in bringing the premier to the conclusion to offer Mr. Sutherland the portfolio of Public Works. In addition, he was probably greatly influenced by a consciousness that Mr. Sutherland is peculiarly well qualified for the duties of his new office. It is well known that during late years Sir Wilfrid Laurier has learned to place great confidence in Mr. Sutherland's business capacity and sound judgment, and in entrusting to him the greatest spending department of the government he feels that he is placing it in hands that will not betray the trust. Mr. Sutherland's long tenure of office of chief Liberal whip brought him in close relationship with the members of both parties, and he is to-day one of the most popular men in parliament.
I am very sorry my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) is not present.

Yes, he is here.
Mr. MONK, (reading).
He is gifted with many of the qualities that go to make a successful administrator. Forceful yet urbane, possessing great capacity for work, and having an intimate knowledge of the Dominion its resources and its requirements, he is well equipped to give the Public Works Department a business-like administration.
Now comes the gloomy side:

It is to be regretted that the appointment of Mr. Raymond Prefontaine to the portfolio vacated by Mr. Sutherland is unlikely to be received with equal favour. There has been much debate over this matter, and it is to be assumed that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, finding himself confronted by a serious political crisis in his own province, has turned to Mr. Prdfontaine as a popular and hitherto successful local leader, and one who, under much provocation, has shown a consistent loyalty to his chief. Those who have discountenanced Mr. Prfifon-taine's selection for this office did not under value the qualities which fit him for leadership, and which evidently appealed very strongly to Sir Wilfrid Laurier under present conditions. While thoroughly sympathizing with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, however, it is not for those Liberals who have observed Mr. Prefon-taine's career as the practical head of the administrative machinery of the city of Montreal to feel that his selection for the head of an administrative department of the government satisfies their ideals of what ought to be. The ' Herald ' particularly, during a five years' campaign against corruption and extravagance at the city hall, had no option but to conclude that his powerful influence had been and was being exerted against the city's best interest.
What Mr. Prdfontaine's idea of his future may be, and precisely what view Sir Wilfrid Laurier may take of the matter, is not for us to know, but it is clear that in Montreal, where he has lived under the lime light of publicity, there must be grave misgivings concerning the wisdom of the selection, not only on the part of the more or less disinterested general public, but quite as much on the part of those whose particular concern is the welfare of the administration.
The article of the ' Witness,' I think, was even more pointed than this one. If I cite these articles, and particularly this one taken from a government organ whose very existence depends upon the existence of this government, it is in order to show that long before we went into that election campaign in Maisonneuve, that that question was agitating the public mind, and the impression gained ground that my right hon. friend, divided between two strong conflicting forces, had compromised himself, had been an opportunist once more, and had given the Department of Public Works to my hon. friend who occupies that position at the present moment, and had entrusted a department, a spending department, but a far less important department, in the judgment of the general public, to my right hon. friend who presented himself for election before the electors of Maisonneuve. Well, Sir, there were two issues before the great electorate of that division, two issues only. My hon. friend the member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) to-day, we understood had parted from the present government, not as a man who elects a seat on the bench, not as a man who is translated to some other office, not as one whose portfolio had become vacant by death or other accident; but he had parted from this government upon a great question of principle, upon a question which we have been discussing in this House to an almost un-

limited extent since we met in the month of March last. That hon. gentleman claimed that the protection afforded to manufacturers was insufficient, and that was one of the issues raised in that campaign. We who believe that the protection afforded to the industrial life of this country is insuflfcient, deemed it to be our duty to go down before the electorate and defend the views to which we have given expression more than once since we have assembled in this session of parliament. I admit, Mr. Chairman, that upon that issue we were unsuccessful, and I am prepared to say, what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said very often since, that those most interested perhaps in the principles which we defended, seemed to think that their only hope of escaping punishment by this government was to elect my hon. friend the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who absolutely promised them sufficient protection for every one of the industries represented in that great constituency. We had gone into the constituency of Argen-teuil, and we had heard the doctrine of free trade preached there ; and I understand that in the electoral division of Yarmouth, that doctrine was also preached in still less uncertain language. But in the electoral division of Maisonneuve those who, I think, should have supported the principles which we defended, deemed it expedient under the circumstances to elect my hon. friend, not in the hopd that the principles which he advocated there would prevail, but with the expectancy that at least their interests would not be completely sacrificed after the promises which my hon. friend distinctly made to them.
That was one issue, Mr. Chairman, but there was another to which I must come at once, because it is an issue which Is concerned with the argument which I shall lay before the committee. In the division of Maisonneuve we heard this argument : That my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) having quitted the government because of differences which had arisen between him and the government was no reason why we should be deprived in the city of Montreal of the portfolio of Public Works-not on racial or religious ground.
Hear, hear.
My hon. friend (Mr. Le-mieux) says ' hear, hear.' What does he mean by that ?
Hear, hear.

Not on any narrow ground suoh as that, but because we claimed in the city of Montreal, and this has been stated here time and again within the hearing of every hon. member of this House, that important works were in process of execution, works which were under the control of the Department of Public Works
and there was no reason why we, in that district, and the people of the province of Ontario should be deprived of that department because, forsooth, as expressed in this article in the ' Herald ' which I have just read, and there were many; others; the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and a certain number of his friends had no confidence in the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prfifontaine). That is what we claimed and so strong was that claim, that, as my friends from the province of Quebec are well aware, being a just and equitable claim, it was re-echoed throughout the whole press of the province, and if I wished to convince the committee of the truth of what I am saying, I would have to spend part of the afternoon reading quotations from newspapers, Liberal and Conservative alike, wherein it was claimed that it was an unfortunate matter that the right hon. Prime Minister of this Dominion had deprived the province of Quebec and the people under whose very eyes these works of improvement in the port of Montreal, in Quebec, and in the St. Lawrence were being executed, of this department at a moment, when, in the judgment of these people, that department should have remained under the control of a minister from their own province. In other words, we laid down the proposition that the people of the province of Quebec were not concerned with what certain members of the Liberal party must think of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, they were not concerned with the pressure which had been brought to bear on the government not to admit him to the department, but they had done nothing to deserve the deprivation of the services of that department This feeling found manifestation in the vote of the electorate. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will not deny that that was one of the great grounds urged during the election. He knows it and so do all those who participated in the campaign. How was that argument met V I was not present in this Chamber the other day when the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) read the verbatim report of the first speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries in that campaign, but, without taking up uselessly the time of this committee, I appeal to any hon. member of this House from the province of Quebec to state whether it is not a fact that the hon. member for Maisonneuve, in every single public utterance which he made during that campaign availed himself of the opportunity to state what, Sir ?-to state that he bad accepted the Department of Marine and Fisheries upon one condition, and that was that everything which concerns transportation, to use his own language, from the extreme west to the Atlantic ocean, every expenditure connected with the carrying out and executing of the works of improvement of the St. Lawrence

was going to be placed under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. He argued, and his friends argued, that it was an anomaly that works connected with harbours, dredging and deepening the St. Lawrence, canals, wharfs, and the carrying out of the plans of improvement in the city of Montreal, should be under the control of the Department of Public Works while the attending to lighthouses and buoys should be under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Transportation was one single, simple work according to them which should be under one department, and the government had decided that from the Department of Public Works would be taken everything in regard to the execution of improvements in reference to transportation and placed under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. There were numerous public meetings, there were articles in tihe newspapers, there were private assurances given right and left throughout that campaign, and I defy any one of my hon. friends who observed that campaign to any degree to deny what I have just stated. Why, Sir, if any confirmation were wanted of the description of the campaign which I have just given, surely the members of this committee will find it in the speech from the Throne, because in that speech hon. members will find a repetition of everything that was stated by the liou. Minister of Marine and Fisheries during that campaign in Maisonneuve. Such was the feeling at that time that had my hon. friend come down to the electors of Maisonneuve and stated that it was not the intention of the government to modify in any way the machinery of the department to which he had been called, 1 have no hesitation in saying that the result of that election would have been different. We have proceeded during the sittings of this committee to vote, I believe, hundreds of thousands of dollars to be expended by the Department of Public Works, although, on this side of the House on more than one occasion, the government has been called upon to state to us what are the modifications which are going to be made in the Department of Public Works and if the present election pledges of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries are to be carried out. I believe that the government has put off that announcement by stating that when the time came to introduce legislation in regard to these changes the government would do its duty. What I claim now as one who was present and heard these declarations, and as an elector myself in the electoral district of Maisonneuve is that before voting this money not after, we have the right to know from the government clearly and explicitly, what are the changes that are going to be made, and if the assurance as given by my hon. friend when he came down to Maisonneuve to solicit the votes of the electors were really based upon the faith of this government, Mr. MONK.
and if this government intends carrying out these pledges. 1 certainly under no circumstances w-ould like to fulfil the part of an obstructionist, but I believe we ought to hold firm to the old principles of our constitution, that redress goes before supply.
I claim, Sir, that it is a grievance that we should be called upon to vote money here from day to day, without the government announcing whether or not these changes are going to be carried out. 1 believe that we would be justified on this side of the House, in preventing the voting of further moneys to the Public Works Department, if the government still continues to refuse that information which we are entitled to. We have the constitutional right to know what expenditures which we are voting to the Public Works Department are to be removed to the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I do not at present express any opinion ou the wisdom of these changes in the departments. I do not say that they would be wise, but what I do say is that when we vote this money to be disposed of by a minister of the Crown, we have the right to a distinct assurance from the government, as to whether any reliance can be placed upon the statements of the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Pr6-fontaine) when he sought re-election from his constituents.
For the tenth or twelfth time my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has brought up this question to which he has received an answer, on one occasion at least, if not on more than one.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. It is the first time I brought up this question. I have never mentioned it in the House before.

Well, I have heard that there were dissensions on the other side of the House, and perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) does not now occupy the position he was supposed to hold in his party. His statement seems to confirm the rumours which I have heard that he is not so much a chief of his party as he is supposed to be, because if he has not brought up the question himself it has been brought up by those who sit behind him, and they have been answered. 1 would suppose that an answer given to the hon. gentleman's supporters would have been sufficient for himself, but since we have to take it that there is a division in the party, and that the answer given to his followers is not sufficient for the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), I have no objection to tell him once more. I would not have alluded to these rumours but for the fact that my hon. friend himself is the first to bring rumours into the discussion, and his speech of half an hour was based on rumours which he said were current in the streets of Mont-

real at the time my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was called to the government. He has announced that at that time there were rumours in Montreal to the effect that I was drawn in opposite directions as to who should be the successor in the cabinet of the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte). Let me tell my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that he had better not take too much stock in these rumours. I suppose that representations are always made to a Prime Minister under such circumstances, but the Prime Minister has the responsibility of making the selection, and at all events I followed my own course and my own methods. And. Sir. when I concluded to bring into the government my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Frefontaine) I think I made no mistake.
Hear, hear.

It is true that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and others, supposed that I had made a mistake, but that is not my opinion. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had been a member of this House for a number of years ; he was a leading member of the bar of Montreal ; and he was also prominent in the municipal affairs of the city in which he lives. As it happens, in municipal politics, as in other politics, my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) who was mayor of Montreal, did not give universal satisfaction to everybody. He had opponents ; I do not think he had any enemies, but he had opponents. There were those who did not agree with him in municipal politics, though they agreed with him in federal politics, and perhaps those who disagreed with him in municipal politics thought that I would go beyond the record and seek in the municipal politics of Montreal in order to be guided in the choice I was going to make. I made no such mistake as that.

Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER, I was satisfied with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as a member of the Liberal party. I did not go to seek what had been his record as mayor of Montreal, though had I done so. while I would have found some opposed to him, I would have found thousands of electors in the city of Montreal who were enthusiastic in his support.
Hear, hear.

I have no reason to believe that the choice I then made was a mistaken one. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) tried the issue in Maisonneuve and he knows the result ; he tried the issue in Argenteuii, and he knows the result ; he tried the issue in Terrebonne, and he knows the result ; he tried the issue in Two Mountains, and the verdict was the same over again. It is no wonder that my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) met
with a much deserved rebuke from the people of the province of Quebec. No wonder he was told on four different occasions that the course he followed was the most unpatriotic course that had ever been followed by a public man.
Hear, hear.

Why, Sir, the doctrine was laid down-I think by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) personally, but if not by him personally, it was laid down by his prominent political supporters and at all events it was laid down in his own organ-the doctrine was laid down that in this matter I had betrayed the province of which I am a native. In some of the speeches of those who at that time were his followers, whatever they may be now, the declaration was made that I had betrayed my native province, because forsooth I had called to the Ministry of Public Works, not a man from the province of Quebec, but a man from the province of Ontario. The doctrine laid down by my hon. friend's party, and I think by himself also, that the portfolio of Public Works belonged to the province of Quebec, and that it was betraying the interests of my own province to call to be an occupant of that office, any one but a member coming from the province of Quebec. Now. Sir. I say that on more than one occasion the people of the province of Quebec have shown that they were not to be misled by such low appeals to their prejudices.
Hear, hear.

The people of the province of Quebec are not to be told that this portfolio or that portfolio belongs to such and such a province. In the composition of this cabinet, it matters not where a minister comes from ; whether he comes from this province or that province ; whether it is from that place or from that other place. As chief adviser to His Excellency the Governor General, it is my duty to select a minister, and to select him. who. in my judgment and opinion, is best qualified for the position.
Hear, hear.

When the portfolio of Public Works became vacant by the resignation of my hon. friend from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) I thought that I could not do better than to give it to my hon. friend and colleague ; my old friend : my friend of twenty years association with me in the work of the Liberal party on the floor of this House.
Hear, hear.

I thought that the business ability of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) was such as to enable him to occupy the position of Minister of Public Works, with some credit to himself and some advantage to the country.

Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
Hear, hear.

Shall I be told that this was a betrayal of the interests of my province ? No, Sir ; but still, that was the issue upon which the election of Maison-neuve was fought by my hon. friend and his party. Now, Sir, two years ago there was a change in the composition of the cabinet. Two years ago the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Mills, was called to the bench of the Supreme Court, and a good appointment it was. I thought it advisable to recommend to His Excellency the successor of Mr. Mills, a gentleman from the province of Quebec, the present Minister of Justice i Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick), and a good appointment it was also. Was there ever a rumour, a murmur, in the province of Ontario that by so doing I was betraying the province of Ontario ? There was not a murmur. It was admitted on all hands that the present holder of the portfolio was worthy of it. Nor has a word been said against the qualification of my hon. friend the present Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) for the position he occupies. Not a word would be said against that appointment even in the province of Quebec ; and when my hon. friend goes to the province of Quebec and tries to repeat what he has done before, tries to rouse the prejudices of the province, he will not do it at the expense of the present Minister of Public Works.
I cannot let my hon. friend state things which are not correct. I have never tried to rouse the prejudices of the province of Quebec.

Here is what was said :	There was a meeting at Three
Rivers at which the hon. gentleman was present. It was a great pow-wow of the party, a rally to assert the principles of the great Liberal-Conservative party in the province of Quebec. My hon. friend was there as the leader of the party. I have not his speech, unfortunately ; but I have the speech of one of his prominent followers, the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), and this is what that hon. gentleman said :
I will stand by it.
I will quote it in French, and then try to translate it into English :

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Le ministfere des Pdcheries peut avoir une eertaine importance par suite du contrdle qui lui est donne des grandes pScheries des cdtes des deux oedans, importance qui a <ste de beau-coup diminuee par le recent jugement du Con-seil PrivS ; quant au departement de la Marine a part la construction et l'entretien des phares, des bouees et des lumiSres, il n'a de jurisdiction, d'aprds le statut de 1892, que sur des sujets qui donnent au titulaire peu d'influence et de prestige.
*	Sic	*
Par l'action de Sir Wilfrid Laurier, le parti liberal a subi une humiliation, la province de Quebec, est bafouee, et M. Prefontaine, en ra-massant cette pitance que lui ont jet6e ses nouveaux eollSgues, a montrd qu'il n'a pas la moindre fiertS personnelle, ni le moindre sentiment de 1'honneur national.
My hon friend says the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries may have a certain importance, but it is only of minor importance. Then he goes on to say :
By the action of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Liberal party has been subjected to humiliation, the province of Quebec has been mocked, and Mr. Prdfontaine, in stooping to take the sop which his new colleagues have thrown to him, has shown not the slighest personal dignity nor the slightest feeling of national honour.
If this is not an appeal to the lowest prejudices of the people of the province of Quebec, I do not know what would be ; and this was said in the presence of the leader of the party, who now protests that he never appealed to the prejudices of the people of the province of Quebec. If there is anything that can stamp the conduct of the hon. gentleman, it is the language which I have just quoted, which was spoken in his presence, and to which he never took the slightest exception. This is the sort of warfare to which we have been subjected in the province of Quebec. I called upon my hon. friend the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries to take the portfolio. I was in poor health at the time ; I had to leave immediately for the south ; but I told him that in my opinion the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries ought to be reconstructed, so as to give it a more extended jurisdiction on matters purely nautical than it had at that time. I am not aware what my hon. friend said in his election ; he is here to speak for himself ; but as to the question put by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), since he was not in the House to hear the answer given a few days ago by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, and since his colleagues behind him have not taken him sufficiently into their confidence as to inform him, I will now tell him that all the appropriations asked for by the Minister of Public Works shall be expended by him.
I am very sorry that my right hon. friend has given to this discussion a direction which I think is wrong.
Oh, oh.

I do think so. I asked a question in regard to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, to which my right hon. friend has given no answer. He admits, or seems to admit, that we have a right to information. He would not go so far as to deny that principle, but he satisfies himself with launching out against me, the most unjustifiable inuendoes. In a few muttered sentences which he utters with reference to the present incumbent of the office of Minister of Public Works, he states that the appropriations which we are at present voting will be expended under that gentleman's supervision. Now, I ask anybody if that is the pledge which was given by all those who supported my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the campaign of Maisonneuve. Is that a categorical answer ? No ; my right hon. friend knows perfectly well that what I stated in the campaign in Maisonneuve was true, that neither the Minister of Public Works nor any other member of this government would dare to come down into the county of Maisonneuve and confirm what my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries there stated. When my hon. friend was defied to produce a letter or a telegram from the right hon. leader of the government, or from any of his colleagues to the effect that the platform upon which he rested his election was approved by the government, that defiance was never accepted ; and we have the proof to-day, if proof was wanted, that the pledges given by my hon. friend the Min-inster of Marine and Fisheries had no authority, and that there will be no such change in the department as my hon. friend stated that the government had decided upon. It is all very well for the right hon. leader of the government, who is surrounded by men who cannot think of anything but to applaud what he says, to come before this committee and impugn what I stated before the electors of my province. I leave these electors to appreciate the value of the indictment brought by my right hon. friend; but I wish to say to him that the accusation which he has formulated against me can very well be turned against himself and against his friends in that province. Since 1896, and before that time-and my right hon. friend knows it well-we have not been able to have an election in the province of Quebec without those very appeals which my right hon. friend charges me with making. And in the by-election referred to by my hon. friend, he has the audacity to say that the position I took in the province of Quebec, deserved castigation.
You got it.

Well, it was after I made a speech before the Cartier Club of Montreal that my huge friend from Guysborough went before his electors and dared to say that the speech I had made was the most disloyal and unpatriotic speech ever made.
On that occasion, as on many others, my hon. friend spoke about things of which he knew nothing. But let me return to the indictment of my right hon. friend. I appeal to any one who has followed the byelections in the province of Quebec, referred to by him, to say whether those elections were not carried on, in his behalf, purely and solely upon the race cry. There was no other appeal made by hon. gentlemen opposite. In the division of Maisonneuve- and I speak on my responsibility as a member of this House-how was the canvass carried on ? Why, the Montreal ' Herald ' declared editorially that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had, on more than one occasion, deserved the censure of the ratepayers of Montreal, and pointed out the manoeuvres which were resorted to during that election. The electors were visited at night and asked whether they were going to vote for Mr. Labelle or for that great representative of the French Canadian race, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. And when, Sir, an elector would inquire whether my right hon. friend was a candidate for the division, he was told: ' He is not exactly a candidate, but you know Prfifon-taine is nothing, Sir Wilfrid is everything. He is really the man you are voting for.' Sir, until the Liberals are prepared to discuss in the province of Quebec political questions upon their merits, free from such appeals, it will be very difficult for any man In that province not to receive what my right hon. friend calls castigation.
And majorities.

Call it what you like, but I say that it is deplorable that in my own native province, where the few deliverances which I have made since 1900 have been written out and printed and are not subject in any way to the criticism referred to-I say that it is deplorable that in that great province we are moving towards a state of things when any fair discussion of political questions will become impossible.

Oh, oh.
Mr. MONK-and our great institutions for which we have done so much will not be able to work properly.
Thank you for the province.
Let me tell my hon. friend, who has made those appeals very often himself

Never.
Mr. MONK-that if my right hon. friend should transfer his leadership to somebody else, the hon. member for Gaspfi, who is essentially a time-server, will be quite prepared to transfer his laudation to whomever may be then chosen. I am not making these remarks for the purpose of disparag-

ing my native province. Very far from it. But we can understand the strength of the bonds of blood, and I say that to take an unfair advantage of this sentiment to stifle free discussion is not the proper direction to give to political struggles in that province, and the day will come when my hon. friends opposite, who now use there uo other argument, will find that they have brought about for their own selfish purposes, a state of affairs which will not redound to the good or the advantage of my native province.

I know, Mr. Speaker, this speech of the hon. leader of the opposition in the province of Quebec almost off by heart, because I have heard it many times. I heard it repeated ad nauseam during three or four weeks in the county of Terrebonne and particularly in the county of Two Mountains. My hon. friend treats us all the time to the same theme, namely, the sacrifice of the province of Quebec, because the portfolio of Public Works was given to the hon. minister who now holds it. He continually rings the changes on the sacrifice, as he calls it, of our compatriots in the province of Quebec. From meeting to meeting, from caucus to caucus, and from street corner to street corner, we hear this complaint continually harped upon.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine).

speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that he never came to any of our meetings.

I took good care to keep away from them. But before citing to the hon. gentleman his own words, which he seems to have forgotten, and which were published in his own organ, the ' Journal,' of Montreal, let me once for all say in this House a word in reply to what has been so often repeated regarding my municipal career. For nearly eighteen years I have been a member of the city council of Montreal. Previous to that time, I was mayor of the municipality of Hochelaga, before that municipality was annexed to the city of Montreal. I have always been elected by acclamation by my fellow-citizens, and after serving eighteen years in the city council, my fellow-citizens of Montreal, without distinction of party, creed or nationality, elected me as their chief magistrate by acclamation. Had my career been so bad as some pretend, it would have been easy, in a large city like Montreal, to find somebody to oppose me. But no one dared present himself, and I was left peaceably in possession of the chair of mayor of Montreal during two years. At the expiration of my term of two years, I was again elected for another term, and I may say, without being boastful or showing pride of any kind, that 1 could have been reelected in 1902 during my absence in Europe, had I so desired.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There was a good deal of uncertainty about that.

Well, I am simply stating facts which I think can stand any attempt at contradiction by my hon. friend. My career in the municipal council was attacked daily and is being constantly attacked even now. In this House frequent allusions are made to it. But let me read only a few lines from an article published in ' La Patrie ' on September 20, 1897, when I was about to be a candidate for the mayoralty :
Mr. Pechevin Prefontaine est notre prochain maire. Ses nombreux amis l'ont prie de se porter candidat aux Elections prochaines, et il a accepts croyons a nous.
Alderman Prefontaine will be our next mayor. His numerous friends have asked him to be a candidate in the next elections and he has accepted, we do believe.
Cette nouvelle sera accueillie avec loie par tous les contribuables de notre grande ville.
The news will be received with rejoicing by all the tax-payers of our great city.
Voilh plus de vingt ans que M. Prdfontaine est mgle aux choses municipales et qu'il s'est pour ainsi dire identifiy avec la prospdrite et le progrSs de Montreal.
For more than twenty years Mr. Prefontaine has been connected with municipal affairs, and he has identified himself with the prosperity and progress of Montreal.
II a StS maire d'Hoehelaga avant que cette municipality ne fut annexes a la ville et depuis plus do quinze ans il reprgsente le quartier Hochelaga au conseil municipal de Montreal.
He was mayor of Hochelaga before that municipality was annexed to Montreal and for fifteen years he has represented that ward in the Montreal city council.
Grace a son esprit d'initiative, a son travail, a son activity, l'ouest et Pest de Montreal ont 6t6 transformSs ; des ameliorations partout ont St6 faites ; nos rues one Sty pavSes nos Sgouts ont Sty construits, nos pares ont Ste embellis.
Thanks to his spirit of initiative, his work and activity in Montreal from east to west has been transformed. Improvements everywhere have been made, streets have been paved ; our drainage has been improved and our parks have been embellished.
Tout cela a cofitS de l'argent, beaucoup d'ar-gent.
All this has cost money-a great deal of money.
Mais les contribuables sont aujourd'hui tiers de leur ville, parce qu'elle fait l'admiration des ytrangers qui la visitent.
This cost a good deal of money, but our tax payers are now proud of their city because it is the admiration of all outsiders who visit it.
Pryfontaine a travaille a la prospyrite de Montryal avec cette ynergie entrainante que tout le monde lui connalt.
Prefontaine has worked for the prosperity of the city of Montreal with the effective energy that everybody knows him to possess.

Son glSvation a la mairie sera la recompense due a son labeur incessant.
La popularity dont il joult dans les foules ne fera que s'accroitre, quand il occupera le fau-teuil de premier magistrat de notre ville.
His election to the mayoralty will be the due reward of his labour. The popularity he enjoys in the city will be increased when he occupies the mayor's chair.
That is the opinion of my hon. friend the member for St.. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte), written on the 20th September, 1897. It seems that he has changed from the unanimous opinion of the citizens of the city of Montreal-for that I was unanimously acceptable was shown by the fact I have already mentioned, that there was no opposition, and I remained in the mayoralty for two years. I am sorry to have been obliged to bring this up, but I felt it my duty to do so, because the people may be misled by what has been written and said since then. But I think that nobody will be misled when I cite the exact words of the speeches made against me in the campaign which took place in the month of December last in Maison-neuve division. I will take the first meeting, which is reported in ' Le Journal' on the 26th November last. 1't Is entitled ' The battle is in full blast.' We see in this report that Mr. Labelle, who was running against me in that' election, spoke in the presence of the leader of the opposition for the province of Quebec, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). If these utterances of Mr. Labelle were not designed to arouse the national prejudices of one province against another, I do not know the meaning of the words. I translate from the report, which is in French :
Then comes the appreciation of Mr. PrSfon-taine, whose treachery to the province of Quebec cannot be either excused or explained. Of all those whom Sir Wilfrid Laurier asked to accept the succession to Mr. Tarte, Profontaine was the only one who consented to bear upon his shoulders the humiliation to which he was exposing his compatriots. Let him bear the responsibility and let him not try to find elsewhere the reason of the opposition.
I must not give too many citations. It was the same cry everywhere. Every day the same thing was repeated at meetings of Conservative candidates. I have kept a number of these reports and printed appeals to the electors, with sueh lines as ' Treason to the Province of Quebec,' ' The Province of Quebec Betrayed,' and so on-these words often in red letters-distributed at the church doors and circulated in every way, in the hope of arousing the prejudices of the people. Now, let us see what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier says :
Mr. Monk added that it was to be regretted that the portfolio of Public Works was to he taken away from the province of Quebec and from our element, which already is not any too well treated at Ottawa. We have no good reason for the injustice put upon our province, and that injustice so put upon them the elector of Maisonneuve will resent.
Here are the exact words of the member for Jacques Cartier. Why did he pronounce them ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I will answer, as my hon. friend asks me-it is because he is the only one who, under the circumstances, would accept that portfolio.

That is confirmation of what I have been saying. Further citations of the hon. gentleman's words are unnecessary. But let me quote a few words further, for, time and again, the same thing was said, the same speeches were repeated-I had sacrificed the province of Quebec ; I had sacrificed my compatriots; the portfolio which had been held by a member of the majority of the province of Quebec had been given to one who did not belong to that majority. All this was an appeal to the prejudices of the electors of the province of Quebec ; for, as you know, Mr. Chairman, ninety per cent of the electors there are of French origin. That is the meaning of the arguments used to the electors of Maisonneuve by all the Tory speakers that took part in the campaign. Not satisfied with having been crushed by the immense majority which the electors gave me in that election, they carried the same warfare into Two Mountains and Terrebonne, and on every hustings where I met the hon. member for Jacques Cartier there was a repetition of the same argument-the province of Quebec had been sacrificed by the portfolio of Public Works being given to an Ontario man. In the face of these attempts to arouse prejudice in the province of Quebec, had not we a right to try to explain to our people the position of affairs and make them understand the importance of the Department of Marine and Fisheries ?
Well, Mr. Chairman, I did try to explain, and my friends tried to explain that there were anomalies in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, that there were anomalies in the Department of Public Works, and that it would be the aim of the government to try to bring order out of the confusion. What harm was there in that, I would like to know. And when the same announcement was made in the speech from the Throne at the opening of the session, I do not see why there should be so much trouble and discussion unless it is to bring up again the question that has been discussed during those four elections, and particularly during my election. Why, Sir, to hear these gentlemen during my election campaign, you would have thought that the maritime provinces, which in the past have furnished the occupant of the portfolio of Minister of Marine and Fisheries, were degraded, that their people were inferior, because they had been satisfied for thirty years with the small portfolio of Marine and Fisheries. What inferior people they must have been, these people of Nova Scotia

and Prince Edward Island, to have suffered so long the humiliation of filling the portfolio of Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Let me again cite from the language of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, as reported in the ' Journal ' of the 28th of November, 1902. Speaking of myself he said :
He is so well aware of his Inferiority that he has consented to replace Mr. Tarte in the insignificant role of Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But in belittling himself in that way, he is dragging his province along with him in his downfall. And to-day he is powerless to explain that degradation.
* Degradation ' all the time. I am sorry that one of the ex-ministers and one of the leaders of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) is not present in the House to-day, because he would be flattered at being treated in this manner by one of his leaders in this House, at being told that in accepting the portfolio of Minister of Marine and Fisheries he degraded himself. Just imagine, Mr. Chairman, how low he must have fallen. Of course, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier would not dare to go down to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island and repeat language of that kind; but in the province of Quebec, among people who are supposed by a certain class of politicians not to understand political questions very well, such language is quite right and proper, when the aim is to arouse the prejudice of French Canadians against the government, because the Prime Minister had seen fit to confide to my humble self the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries, which is such a degradation to the province of Quebec. Those are the exact words of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, the leader of the opposition in the province of Quebec. If he is not trying to take advantage of a very small issue for political effect, I do not know the meaning of his speeches. Now, hon. gentlemen will find, on referring to ' Le Journal,' a great deal of edification in reading how the provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island must have been degraded, because, ever since confederation, they have furnished the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Now, Sir, a great deal has been said about my declarations. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee unnecessarily, but if, Mr. Chairman, you will refer to my first speech delivered before the Liberal club of the east end of Montreal, after having been sworn in as minister, you will see exactly what my declarations were. I pointed out to the people assembled there the importance of the department, because the cry had already been started. It was not a question of politics, it was purely an attempt to arouse the prejudices of our fellow citizens in Quebec against the government. I went there, and what did I say ? I said that there were certain works, certain functions, which were under Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
the control of the Department of Public Works at the present time, but that their control by that department involved] an anomaly which the government had decided to remedy. For instance, I mentioned the hydrographic survey. I said, gentlemen, how can you explain that the hydrographic survey, which is one of the most important services for the safety of navigation, is today performed partly by the Department of Public Works, from Montreal to Quebec, partly by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, from Quebec to Belle Isle, and partly by the Department of Railways and Canals, from Montreal to Kingston, and again by the Department of Marine and Fisheries from Kingston to and through the lakes ? I said : Why is it that so many accidents are happening to navigation ? When you try to discover the cause of these accidents, you will find that officers of the several departments throw the blame on each other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is the hydrographic survey in the Department of Public Works now, or in the Department of Marine and Fisheries ?

It is as I said, partly in the Department of Public Works, for the section between Montreal and Quebec, partly in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, from Quebec to Belle Isle, partly in the Department of Railways and Canals, from Montreal to Kingston, and again under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, from Kingston to the lakes. Therefore, you have four sections under different control on the one route, the St. Lawrence route. I stated at this meeting that that was an anomaly, that this work should be all under the control either of one department or the other. Arguing from that standpoint, what did I say further ? I pointed out another anomaly in the case of the harbour commissioners. I said that there were three boards of harbour commissioners, one at Quebec, one at Montreal, and one at Three Rivers, all under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries; but when you have any work to perform you must first get the approval of the Department of Public Works. Is it not reasonable to say that the Department of Marine and Fisheries should have something to say about these works, although they might be entirely under the control of the Department of Public Works as regards nominations and so on, since the works were executed with their own money borrowed on the credit of the government ? Still is it not reasonable that the Department of Marine and Fisheries should also have a word to say in the performance of those works ?
They can build a wharf where there Is no water and tihe Department of Marine and Fisheries will have nothing to say about it.

They can build an elevator or anything they wish regarding transportation or navigation without a word of advice to be taken from the Department of Marine and Fisheries. These are the anomalies to which I referred. There are others. There is, for instance, the work of dredging the St. Lawrence and of sweeping the channel. I do not say that these works should be at once transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, because these vast works which have been begun must better be continued under the control of the Department of Public Works. But. surely a public man has a perfect right to discuss these questions and to lay these facts before his fellow citizens. My fellow citizens accepted my view upon these questions. They knew what T had done, they knew from my public record what I could do and what I would do, and they believed me in preference to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier and his confreres who came into the division of Maisonneuve, and notwithstanding what they said about the treachery of the ex-member for Maisonneuve, and notwithstanding that they predicted that I would not be re-elected, my fellow citizens were satisfied to return me'for that division. I went into Terrebonne which 1 had represented and I carried on1 the campaign in the same way as I had done in Maisonneuve. It was stated right and left that the treachery of which I had been guilty would redound against the Liberal party, yet Terrebonne had never, previous to my election returned a Liberal candidate. At the present time you have a Liberal sitting for that division and elected by a larger majority than has ever been given before. These are the facts and these are the results of the speeches of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier and his friends who are trying to rouse the prejudices of the electors of the province of Quebec. I repeat again what has been so ably said by my right hon. leader that the province of Quebec is not led astray by such speeches. It has never been led astray by such speeches-I thank God it has not been-and it never will be. If what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has stated be true that canvassers were going around and asking the electors to vote for the right hon. leader of the government during the last election, that, was a pretty good argument. These canvassers and the people to whom they spoke knew perfectly well who was the candidate and in electing the Minister of Marine and Fisheries they knew that they were electing a faithful and loyal friend of the right ho*, leader of the government and of the Liberal party.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
Surely, Mr. Chairman, I am bound to "say a word or two. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) has just read an article that makes it a duty for me to get on my feet. That article 93	-
which, I apprehend, I never wrote myself, was published in 1897.	1 was a little
younger then than I am now, and I was not in newspaper work as deeply then as I am at the present time. The lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries was then asking the vote of the electors for the mayoralty. But, before talking of our municipal affairs, I would like to say a word or two as to the main question which has been raised. Let me say, first, that I was never of the opinion and that I am not of the opinion today that the portfolio of Public Works, or Marine and Fisheries, or Finance, or any other department, belongs to one province exclusively. We are a mixed community; we are, I hope, building up a nation here. I had the honour to be for nearly six years and a half Minister of Public Works for the whole Dominion, not for the province of Quebec exclusively, but for the whole Dominion. And whatever differences might have arisen between my political friends of former days and myself I believe they will never reproach me, whatever their race may be, with having been partial either towards or against them. The Department of Public Works did not belong exclusively to the province of Quebec. I would have been very glad indeed if it had remained within the province in which it had been for many years. I was so much of that opinion that in spite of the personal differences very well known between my hon. friend the tooii. Minister of Marine and Fisheries and myself, I distinctly stated in ' La Tatrie,' and I had taken full charge of the paper then, that I would have not the slightest possible objection to the hon. gentleman being appointed Minister of Public Works. I stated that publicly and I stated it privately to my hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) himself. But political friends at that time were raising a violent opposition against the appointment of the hon. Minister of Marine. I had nothing more to do with it ; I did not say a word one way or the other.	But there was a
great row raised and a violent agitation took place in the Liberal ranks against the appointment of the hon. member for Maisonneuve. Most of that opposition came, I may say, or a great deal of it at any rate, from those who had been opposed to the hon. gentleman in his municipal career. I do not believe that we are called upon to discuss within this House all our municipal difficulties in Montreal. However, since the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has seen fit to quote an article that was published in ' La Patrie ' six years ago, let me say a word or two on that topic. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries had been for many years Chairman of the Roads Committee of the city of Montreal, and he was mayor for two years.
Four years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I beg my bon. friend's pardon. It is long indeed-very long.
It might have been longer.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It might have been longer, but the city of Montreal decided in another way. Those who were most violently opposed to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries were the strongest Liberals in the city of Montreal. In 1897 he was -elected mayor, and he was elected in 1900 also. I may say that it was very difficult in the past to make any opposition to the hon. gentleman. I am speaking within the hearing of many people from the city of Montreal who took part in the municipal elections. The racial cry was the principal cry that the hon. gentleman used all the time.
I beg to deny in the most formal manner what the hon. gentleman has stated just now. He cannot show a single word from me to that effect. It is all gratuituous. Let him try it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows very well that I am within Gospel truth. There was for a time an English majority in the city council of Montreal. My hon. friend and others made up their minds-I do not blame them-that the French Canadians should have their share, and they started a strong agitation to take hold of municipal affairs. The hon. gentleman made that fight'on the racial cry. He and his friends made that fight on the racial cry for years and years.
I deny it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: My hon. friend may deny it, but I am speaking the truth.
Take it back.
I will accept his *denial in the parliamentary sense, but my words will be read by the whole city of Montreal.
You supported him apparently.
I said it was very *difficult indeed to raise an opposition against him.
You tried.
I tried and I succeeded.
When ?
The strongest Liberals came to ' La Patrie ' and to myself personally, just as they went to the right lion, leader of the government himself ou several occasions and represented to him

that the city of Montreal was being wrecked and was being destroyed. The organization against my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. PrS-fontaine) in municipal affairs was in the ' Herald ' office. The ' Herald ' people came to my office and to me personally. The leaders of the Liberal party in Montreal-I will give the names if I am asked to give names, because there is no secret about it-they came to me and they asked me whether ' La Patrie ' would consent to take a hand in the fight, because they felt that if they had not a French paper to speak to the French electors, it was out of the question to have municipal reform in Montreal. My hon. friend (Hon. Sir. Pre-fontaine) had made an alliance with a certain group in the Conservative party-the ' La Presse ' people-at the time. If there was not a French paper in a position to make a fight against him, a fight was out of the question. I give these explaiwtions so that people will understand how ' La Patrie ' was drawn into those municipal contests. It took us some time before we were able to get municipal reform in Montreal. In 1900, most of the aldermen who had followed my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Pre-fontaine) were defeated ; defeated to a man. He remained the only one of his group in the municipal council. He was allowed to be elected mayor. We had clipped his wings and he was allowed to remain there.
Hear, hear.
In 1902 he tried his level best to be a candidate.
I was not here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman went away, but he placed his candidature before the electorate and he could not be elected and he withdrew. But this is only municipal history, and I would not have alluded to it if I had not been invited by my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. PrSfontaiue) to do so. In 1897, it appears that ' La Patrie ' supported him. In 1900 he was allowed to be elected under the conditions that have been described. In 1902 he was defeated, to his great happiness, because he lias been made a minister since. Now, as to his.last election campaign. There is no doubt whatever that he stated to the electorate that a part of the Public Works Department would be transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. His words have been reported verbatim. What he announced will not be done. That is sufficient for me. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is right on one point, and that is, when he said that the hydraulic survey should be placed in the Marine Department. I share his views ou that point. The reason why the Department of Public Works undertook the survey on the St. Lawrence river between Quebec and Montreal, was because that department was carrying on extensive dredging, and it was necessary to have in-

formation and data, but it was not the intention or ambition to trespass on the rights of any other department. The dredging work is nearly finished now. My hou. friend (Hon. Mr. Prgfontaine) may take over the hydrographic survey if he chooses ; after one more year's work it will be finished. I repeat that there is no sound argument to be invoked in support of the contention that one department should always belong to the same province. My hou. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has alluded to appeals that have, he claims, been made in the elections of 1896 and 1900. There were apepals on both sides. I have read a great many appeals in these two campaigns. I hope we will never hear them again.
Hear, hear.

I hope that in future we will discuss political questions on their merits. The people of this country have grown big enough to discuss political questions on their merits. Let me tell my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that X differ from him on the point that in the province of Quebec we cannot discuss any political question today on their merits because the name of the Prime Minister is supreme. The name of the right hon. gentleman is a powerful name, X am bound to say, in the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear.

I spring from the soil so to speak ; I am the son of a farmer, and I claim that there is enough independence in the hearts, and in the souls, and in the conscience of the French Canadians, whether farmers or workingmen or anything else, to discuss political questions and to understand them as they deserve to be understood. There is no doubt that my right hon. friend's name is a powerful one in the province of Quebec, but I would not be afraid in any way to discuss with him now, as I have in past years, the political questions of the day, and I would not be afraid of the verdict, if I am right.
Hear, bear.
The province of Quebec is equal to the other provinces of this Dominion.
Hear, bear.
We are not carried away by a name, or by prejudices, or by passion. There may be people who are prejudiced, but there are prejudiced people in every part of the Dominion.
Everywhere.

Yes, everywhere. I protest in a friendly way, but as firmly as I can against the assertion that the name of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is so powerful that we cannot with advantage discuss political 93J
questions in our province. The time may come when we may be obliged to discuss these questions with my right hon. friend, and the people of the province of Quebec will listen to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, to myself, to anybody who will appeal to them and give us a fair hearing. I am sure that the words spoken by my bon. friend (Mr. Monk) do not express his real sentiments and views on this question. Now, Mr. Speaker, perhaps we from the city of Montreal, have relied too much on the indulgence of the House in discussing our municipal affairs, but as they are somewhat connected with our political differences it was just as well to settle our case kindly, as I have endeavoured to do.

I have listened with a good deal of attention to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) and I am surprised that he has raised such a breeze in the" House, over ah incident which one would think should have been settled by what occurred here a few days ago. I would not have attempted to speak in this debate, were it not that the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) had made some insinuations with regard to my humble self. He has stated that as a member of the Liberal party, I had appealed to passions and prejudices in the province of Quebec to sustain the Liberal party, or what he termed, the cause of the right hon. leader of the government. I beg to tell my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), in the most respectful manner, in the most courteous manner, speaking from my seat in parliament-and this is the right place to make such a denial -that never in my political life did I make any such appeals as he said I made.
Hear, hear.

I have met the hon. gentleman in four counties where elections were held recently ; I have met him in many political discussions ; and I call upon him now to say if I ever uttered in his bearing such appeals as he has mentioned. I say that I never did. But, Sir, let me show the course which the hon. gentleman has pursued in the province of Quebec for the last four or five years. Last year, speaking on the budget, I quoted tbe remarks which were made by him before the Morin Club, a very piwerful Conservative association in Montreal. I will again quote those remarks, not as reported in ' La Patrie ' or ' La Presse ' or any other French Canadian papers, but as telegraphed to the Toronto 'Mail and Empire,' the chief organ of the Liberal Conservative party in this country. Here is what my hon. friend said, as reported in that paper :
Laurier Fails in Duty to Quebec. His Premiership of No Aid to French Canadians. Notable Speech by F. D. Monk.
And the ' Mail ' goes on to say :
By the very nature of his position Sir Wilfrid Laurier was obliged every day to make conces-

sions. In the same way when the subsidies to the provinces came up for consideration, Prince Edward Island received a bonus. New Brunswick will also receive one, but Quebec's claims are left without consideration. The same thing applied to experimental farms. Every other province had one, but Quebec was left out. In the Immigration Department, conducted by Mr. Sifton, the French Canadians were practically eliminated. The immigration was directed to the far west, to the detriment of Quebec. Referring to the Montreal harbour works, Mr. Monk said that the necessary works have been delayed for years simply because the government is afraid to do anything for the province of Quebec, which gives Canada its Prime Minister. All along the line Mr. Monk claimed that Quebec province had gained nothing, but, on the contrary, had lost in prestige and advantages by having one of its own sons at the head of the government.
This is the language used by my kon. friend in every political campaign in our province, and he dares to state before this House that we, the members of the Liberal party, are raising racial issues against his own party, when, as I have clearly demonstrated, we have to answer such arguments as these on the platform. Sir, I have met lately the hon. gentleman in the county of Maisonneuve, and in the county of Terrebonne, and I am bound to say for the edification of this House, that this is the kind of language used by my hon. friend when he speaks to the French Canadian electors. I have here the verbatim report of the speech made by him shortly after the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries was called to office. He was speaking at Three Rivers on Friday, the 14th of November last. I will translate it. This is what he sand :
What a spectacle Is now offered to us ! Of what are we sorrowful witnesses ? You see the most important department of the government taken away from the province of Quebec. If Mr. Tarte has administered his department in a fair and proper way, why cannot there be found an honest man to succeed him ?
That is the way the hon. gentleman spoke of liis own province and our public men.
Why have they chosen the occasion when there are so many public works here and in Montreal to he undertaken, to take away the department from us ? The reason for the hesitation which has attended the appointment of Mr. Tarte's successor, is that Mr. Sutherland was contending that the province of Ontario was entitled to the department. Why has not Mr. Prdfontaine insisted that this department should be dismantled, and why has he not defended our rights ?
Sir, til is is the verbatim speech delivered by the hon. gentleman at the moment the hon. member for Maisonneuve was called to the cabinet. I was present also when the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries made his speech before the Liberal Club of Montreal East, and what did he state ? Did he state in a formal manner that the Department of Public Works would be merged in the Department of Marine and Fisheries ?

Sir, I state here boldly that he did not. I heard what he said, and I listened carefully. He stated that at an informal meeting held the day previous with his colleagues, he was asked by them to make a report on the feasibility of a scheme to merge a part of the Department of Public Works into the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Will my hon. friend allow me ?
Yes.

This is what my hon. friend himself stated in an interview in 'La Presse:'
As an old fighter I congratulate him on his nomination. I do not know the intentions of the government on the subject of the changes which are to be made in the ministry of Public Works. If the modifications announced are made, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries must become very important. I hope sincerely that they will take place, because the St. Lawrence route, in which the province of Quebec is so interested, will benefit thereby.
Hear, hear.

Sir, I am reported faithfully, and I will not take one word from that interview. It is true, and I hope it will be found to be true at the end. But really my hon. friend is too old a parliamentarian to revive such dead issues. Does he fancy for the moment that there are not enough reporters, journalists and telegraph officers in this country to record what is being stated by public men during a political campaign ? Let me warn my hon. friend that each time he speaks in the province of Quebec, as he has spoken during the last six or seven years, he will be faithfully reported at least by the Liberal press of Canada if not by the Conservative press.
Hear, hear.

We aTe charged to-day by hon. gentlemen ; who, with their political ancestors, have for the last half century been raising in our province political issues of a racial and religious character. I appeal to the old parliamentarians who sit around me ; I appeal to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) who has stood the brunt of the battle for nearly half a century.
Hear, hear.

Let him recall to this House how the French Canadian Liberals, who have borne the battle in the days gone by were treated by their Conservative opponents. Sir, for a number of years the Liberals in the province of Quebec were ousted from public life, nay, even from the church. They could not appear on a political platform." They were branded as bad Catholics and as enemies of society. But slowly and slowly the truth came out. They had a great leader in the person of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. In him we

had a man who appealed, not to the prejudices of his race, but to their intelligence and their conscience, and he made the name of Liberal respected throughout that province, as it is to-day throughout the Dominion. To-dtiy we are no more ousted from the church, we are respected by the powers that be, notwithstanding the unchristian, the unpatriotic attitude of the leaders of the Conservative party towards us. We all have learned, through the great lessons taught by our leader, the value of civil rights. But my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) I understand, has raised this debate in order not to let his hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) take the lead. We all know that to be the case. It is, as we say in French, ' un secret de Polichinelle,' it is secret which is running about every street in Montreal that my hon. friend from Montmorency is the would-be successor of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), and the latter asserted this afternoon his leadership by bringing up an old issue which had already been thrashed out the other day.
