You are probably not aware, Sir, that after the election which took place during the months of November and December last, the leading Conservative organ in Montreal, ' Le Journal,' which was then his organ, but which has since veered around and transferred its allegiance and support to my hon. friend from Montmorency, informed him plainly that he could not continue to act as the leader of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec, unless he changed his political tactics. It is 'well known that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has been disavowed by a section of his own party, and by the official organ of that party, and this explains why we are assisting to-day at this little comedy. Yesterday it was my hon. friend from Montmorency who took the lead by bringing up in the House the Treadgold question, and to-day my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier reasserts his title to the leadership by this attack on the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, notwithstanding the fact that my friend from Montmorency brought the same question before the House a few days ago. But I must say this of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier-and I say it in all seriousness-that he enjoys the confidence of his small but gallant phalanx of followers in the province of Quebec, and that, in my opinion, his rival, the hon. member for Montmorency, will not succeed in ousting him from the leadership.

I do not rise, Mr. Speaker, to answer at very great length, the rather impassioned address just delivered by my hon. friend from Gaspe, who seems to have a grudge against either the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) or myself.
Not at all, you are my best friends.

My hon. friend got rather excited and angry, for what reason I am not aware, except that he was anxious to follow the lead of my right hon. friend the First Minister and make an appeal on the same lines. But let me tell my hon. friend from Gaspe that these personal attacks come with very bad grace, especially from him, because if we desired to be disagreeable we could refer back to an election which he went through in Gaspe and bring up again some incidents in that election which would certainly not tell to his credit. But I do not propose to go into such personal matters nor do I propose to rake up ancient history, as my hon. friend did when he talked of the times when, according to him, the Liberals in the province of Quebec were ousted from the church by the Conservatives. I shall content myself with going back to the general elections which took place in 1896, during which the chief argument used by hon. gentlemen opposite and their friends in the province of Quebec was that the late Conservative government had got this House to vote $3,000,000 for the purpose of buying-rifles and enlisting French Canadians to fight the battles of the empire. From parish to parish they went, trying to hound down the Conservatives because, they said,
' you voted $3,000,000 to buy rifles with which to arm our sons and send them to fight the battles of England in a distant land.' Would my hon. friend not call that an appeal to race and prejudice ? And I might point to an hon. minister opposite me who, though he is not given to raising his voice in discussion in this House, is most vehement on the hustings, and was one of the most guilty parties in this instance. Nor will I give more than a passing reference to an argument used in the election of 1900, by prominent gentlemen on the other side who came to fight me in that election, and whose principle argument was that the candidate they were opposing was born in Ontario and spoke English almost as well as French and sent his son to an English Protestant institution. Would my hon. friend not call that an appeal to racial prejudice ? Yet hon. gentlemen who were guilty of such appeals try to lecture us on this side because forsooth, in the exercise of our duty and of our rights, we say that the province of Quebec was humiliated when the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) accepted the portfolio of Minister of Marine and Fisheries instead of insisting on being given the portfolio of Public Works, left vacant by the resignation of the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte). We say that in taking that sop, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries humiliated his province. I have no need to rise here to explain the words which my right hon. friend the Premier read from the speech I made in Three Rivers. These words require no justification at my hands. I stand by what I there said, and I defy my right hon. friend

to quote one sentence in any speech I have ever delivered in any part of this country of which I need be ashamed before this House. And that is more than my right hon. friend and a great many who sit around him can say. Dare they repeat what they said at Chicoutimi and other places in the province of Quebec during the elections of 1896 and 1900 ? I defy them to do it. I say again let them read, if it is not too fatiguing for them, the report of any speech I ever made either in the province of Quebec or in the province of Ontario and quote any sentence for which I need blush before my colleagues in this House or the people of Canada. What is the position I took in the speech I made at Three Rivers. I said that ever:	since 1878 the portfolio of
Public Works had been held by a minister from the province of Quebec, that it was one of the most important in the gift of the Governor General and the Prime Minister, and that it had been in the hands of a French Canadian of the province of Quebec ever since that year. I said that this department had been ably administered by the minister who had just vacated it, and that, under the circumstances, it was the bcunden duty of the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve to insist, as a condition of his entering the government at all, on being given that department. I further said, Sir, that if I had been in his place I would not have accepted the humiliation of taking an inferior department-
Oh, oh.

Yes, Sir, I repeat it-the humiliation of taking an inferior department. I would have insisted upon having the Department of Public Works or one of the other most important departments in the gift of my right hon. friend. What further did I say? I said that it looked very strange, remembering what the ' Herald ' had said, remembering what the ' Witness ' had said, and what must have been said to my right hon. friend the leader of the government in relation to the past career of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-it looked very much as if my right hon. friend would not trust the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with any great spending department. And I declared that that was one of the causes for the humiliation of the hon. gentleman, and it became the humiliation of the province of Quebec in his person, when he accepted the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which is not an important department compared with the Department of Public Works, and is not a great spending department. These were the sentiments to which I gave expression. I have nothing to be ashamed of in them, and I repeat them here before the House in the hearing of my colleagues, and I know I shall have their support.

Mr. Chairman, when you rose at six o'clock, I really had not very much more to say upon the subject which is occupying the attention of the committee, but still, in view of what has been said it seems to me that this discussion can be continued for some minutes more

so as to get from tlie government what we have been trying to get for some time-a specific declaration of what is the policy of the government upon the important question as to whether or not the Department of Public Works is to be divided between the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Public Works. Of course, after the very lucid explanation which was given here this afternoon by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) probably the committee is enlightened and we should not say any more. On the other hand it seems to me that the government is bound to state whether or not the declarations made by the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries on an important occasion are to be carried out by the government; in other words, whether the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries was really authorized to make the statements which he did make. I noticed that both the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries anil the hon. member for Gaspd (Mr. Lemieux), when they spoke about this question, were not ve -y "definite in the expression of their opinions as to what rct.'.ly was to lie done. The right hon. leader of this House (lit. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Dnurier) also spoke, but we fail to find in anything which he said a definite policy laid down by him as to what really was "to be done. When my hon. friend quoted what he said at this meeting of the Liberal club, or Le Club Liberal de la Partie-Est, I think it is, I noticed that he did not quote what is here put in his mouth by the newspapers of Montreal. I want to know if he repudiates the report of his speech which was given both by ' La Patrie ' and ' La Presse ' on that occasion, because both of these reports are identical in terms. Now, my hon. friend, as I read to the House the other night, said, in fact, this ;
Gentlemen, let us be reasonable, let us examine the situation as it is. The Department of Public Works at this moment are spending several millions of dollars. This sum is spent in public buildings and their maintenance, including the parliament buildings at Ottawa, and in the construction of new buildings inv every part of the country where they are needed. Moreover, the Department of Public Works until now has had the dredging of rivers, has carried on the improvements in the port of Montreal, with the assistance, of course, of the harbour commission and of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But if we put every man in his place, and if we. say to the Department of Public Works, not only by words but by deeds, you shall only have under your control the works on the public buildings and the public improvements which relate to the maintenance of the country, hut everything which concerns navigation, such as dredging the rivers, the construction of wharfs, the construction of elevators, the building of dry docks, and so on, if we say that all this concerns navigation and therefore concerns the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and if you put this into a law, is it not true that you have there all the guarantees which you can desire ? But you are told : This is to make the province of Quebec believe that you are not sacrificed. Well, gentlemen, again I repeat, let us be reasonable. If I tell you as I have already said twice, that I have accepted the portfolio under these conditions.
I will call tlie attention of the committee to this ;
And, gentlemen, again I repeat, let us he reasonable. If I tell you, as I have already said twice, that I have accepted the portfolio under these conditions and that they have been sanctioned, It is because I sincerely believe the promises which have been made, the declarations which have been made, and it is because I am sincerely convinced that these promises and declarations will be realized.
So there are the words which were pronounced by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He distinctly said that all those works which are now under the control of the Department of Public Works were to be under bis department. He went farther than that. He said :	These are the conditions under which I accept the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries and these are the sanctioned declarations that I have authority for making to the country. These are the conditions under which I accepted office, and if these conditions had not been granted I would not have accepted. But, there is the indefinite statement that we have now-before the committee. We have this statement simply from my hon. friend who spoke tins afternoon that probably the hydrographic survey which is now in part under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries would be placed wholly under the control of this department. If the hon. gentleman had not come to the electors of the province of Quebec with the distinct statements he made in this speech, the result of the election in Maisonneuve would have been different from what it was when he was elected. It is strange, after what the right hon. leader of the House said this afternoon, if he had decided from the outset to take iDto his cabinet the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that it took so long to come to a decision, because it is in the remembfance of everybody that it took three weeks before my hon. friend was taken into the cabinet. And why, Sir ?-because it is well known also that deputation after deputation came up here to Ottawa to urge that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries be not taken into the cabinet, but that the hon. gentleman who sits here as speaker of this House (Hon. Mr. Brodeur) should be appointed one of the ministers of the Crown. Here is the ' Herald ' of Montreal, not a Conservative organ, not one which is favourable to this side of the House, but one of the great organs of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, and it went so far as to publish the portrait of Mr. Speaker and to say :
The ' Herald ' is to-day in a position to state that the Hon. L. P. Brodeur, member for Rou-ville, and Speaker of the House of Commons, will probably succeed Hon. Mr. Tarte as Minis-

ter of Public Works in the cabinet of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
There is no doubt whatever that there was great wrangling in the Liberal ranks at that time. Deputation after deputation came to Ottawa to urge upon the Prime Minister that he should take into the cabinet the Speaker of this House (Hon. Mr. Bro-deur) and not the member for Maisonneuve (Hon. Mr. PrSfontaine). We were told some time ago that a definite statement would be made to the House as to the policy of the government on this matter, and why is it that such a statement is so long delayed ? I take it, Sir, that the Department of Public Works, having been given to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), it will not be divided now, and that the hon. gentleman is a believer in the motto ' what we have we'll hold.' I suppose that the government should decide to take the Public Works from my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), or suppose they should now propose to diminish the importance of that department, I put it to gentlemen on the other side .of the House, if the members from the other provinces, and especially from Ontario, would not resent such a change. There is nothing extraordinary in the views which I gave expression to, and which were quoted by the Prime Minister to-day. The province of Quebec had for a long time control of the Department of Public Works, and I simply expressed the views of one province at the change that had been made. I feel certain that were that department taken from the province of Ontario to-day we would hear the same protest from Ontario. In the Montreal ' Gazette ' of November 12tli, the Minister of Marine was interviewed, and this is the report of the interview :
' Will there be any new functions added to the Department of Marine and Fisheries ' asked the reporter.
' Yes,' said the hon. gentleman, ' but that cannot be done until parliament meets and the change is ratified by the people's representatives. You see the duties of the several portfolios are at present defined by Act of the central legislature, so nothing short of an amending Act of parliament can affect the change. The St. Lawrence river works will be added to the Marine Department.'
I call the attention of the House to the fact that this interview has never been repudiated. The Minister of Marine continued :
' That will give us the service of building and maintaining our wharfs in the different waters of the Dominion. This will give my department the oversight of what is commonly known as transportation. I have had some opportunity for a study of the subject and I will give it more.' With regard to his Montreal critics Mr. PrSfontaine remarked that he had nothing to say at present but time will show them. I am not the man they have represented me to be.'
That is a corroboration of the speech made by the hon. gentleman, but that is not all.

Never before was the Liberal-Conservative party so united in its opposition to the gentlemen who sit upon the treasury benches. Never before was it so united in word and.in deed, in the performance of the duty which it believes it owes to the people of Canada. If hon. gentlemen opposite can take any comfort from street rumours as to differences which exist between my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) and myself, they are easily satisfied. When my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), in 1900 was the unanimous choice of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec as their leader, I was one of the first to sanction that choice, and I welcomed it as a sure sign of victory at the next election.
Other hon. MEMBERS. Oh.
Oh.

Yes, and my hon. friends on the other side know that what I am saying is true ; they feel it in their bones. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk), since being elected leader of the Quebec Liberal-Conservatives, has grown in the estimation

and respect of every man in this House, and every man in the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) deservedly has the esteem and respect of this House, and I can tell hon. gentlemen opposite, if they do not know it, that he has no more devoted follower than 1 am. My hon. friend from Gasp<5 (Mr. Le-mieux) says I have ambitions. Sir, I have no ambition to be either the leader of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec or the leader , of the district of Quebec. I have not the time, I have not the means, and especially I have not the ability to be leader, even if I so desired. But. Sir, I am honoured in being an humble and ardent and zealous supporter of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier.	'
Hear, hear.

I feel compelled to say a few words in this, in some respects unfortunate debate, because early in the session I entered my protest against the removal from the province of Quebec of such an important department as Public Works, which had been presided over for many years by a member from that province. I agree that no province in Canada owns any particular portfolio, but I do say that the two great provinces of Ontario and Quebec have for many years been recognized as entitled to a fair share of the departments which control patronage and the expenditure of public money. These provinces represent the great majority of the taxpayers of Canada, and it is only right that they should have representation in some degree commensurate with the contributions which they make to the public treasury. Upon the ground, as a business ground, irrespective of parties or nationalities or religions, I think it is a sound principle for a Prime Minister to act upon in forming his government, that the two large provinces of Quebec and Ontario should have strong and prominent representatives in the cabinet. I do not think that will be considered a narrow or prejudiced or debatable ground. Well, there must have been some reason for not carrying out this well-recognized principle in this particular case. The ex-Minister of Public Works, we all agree, had been doing good work, according to his best judgment, and subject to the criticism to which every hon. minister, no matter how good his judgment may be, must be subject. He had been putting a great deal of labour and effort into the work of his department, -with the object of rendering, to the best of his ability, good service to the country in carrying on the operations of that department and in dispensing the enormous patronage which was placed in his hands. The Prime Minister undertook to select a successor to the hon. Minister of Public Works, who had retired, and he took a long
time to decide upon a man. It was not the decision of a moment. He consulted Liberals far and wide ; he was sometimes in Quebec, sometimes in Ottawa, sometimes in Montreal ; possibly he may have consulted business men, some of whom were outside the ranks of the Liberal party. In choosing a successor to the Minister of Public Works, he was not obliged to take the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He had the names of many other hon. gentlemen before him, the Speaker, for instance, and other men quite capable of taking charge of any reasonable portfolio. But the right hon. gentleman saw fit to select the hon. member for Maisonneuve. When he made that choice, he had the record of the hon. gentleman before him. That record was either one which should entitle the hon. gentleman to favour at the hands of the Prime Minister, or it was not. Having been at the head of the municipal public works of the city of Montreal, which is the largest city in Canada, and which has a very large expenditure, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries had certainly been in the very best possible school for fitting a man to fulfil the duties of Minister of Public Works of Canada. Pie had been through the kindergarten experience, which is sometimes a good thing for men to have before entering the cabinet. He had made a record there. If that record was what it ought to have been, the Prime Minister was quite right in selecting him, and be should have given him the Department of Public Works. If that record was not what it ought to have been, the Prime Minister was wrong in taking him into his cabinet at all. As we look over the hon. gentleman's history, which he has made for himself in his native province, as that history is recorded, not by the Conservative press, but by his own friends, we shall be able to understand why the Prime Minister hesitated about placing under that hon. gentleman's control a great spending department like the Department of Public Works. That history has been read here to-day very largely from the Montreal ' Herald,' and it is not necessary for me to go over it again. I will quote, however, what the * Herald ' said on the 10th of November last :
The ' Herald ' particularly, during a five years' campaign against corruption and extravagance at the city hall, had no option but to conclude that his powerful influence had been and was being exerted against the city's best interest. What Mr. Prdfont.aine's idea of his future may be, and precisely what view Sir Wilfrid Laurier may take of the matter, is not for us to know, but it is clear that in Montreal, where he has lived under the limelight of publicity, there must be grave misgivings concerning the wisdom of the selection, not only on the part of the more or less disinterested general public, but quite as much on the part of those whose particular concern is the welfare of the administration.
As I looked over tbe files of tills paper, and found these articles one after another,

beginning in January, 2900, appearing in this leading Liberal organ in the province of Quebec, I saw denunciations against tbe bon. gentleman so bold and daring that their equal could not be found in any paper in Canada, Liberal or Conservative, against any other public man in Canada. The hon. gentleman said to-day that he had acclamations in the city of Montreal, that after he had been elected mayor of the city, he had been continued in that office during four years. Well, here is what the * Herald ' says on his retirement :
The need of the whole city is to he quit of Mr. Prefontaine's domination, and equally to be rid of the system he represents. Prefontaine-ism means the manipulation of the municipal authority for the benefit of those who have business relations with the city, and it means the neglect of public services, the corruption of civic departments, the dissipation of municipal revenues, which result when members of the council extend to themselves the preferential treatment meted out to great corporations.
That is the opinion expressed by the Montreal ' Herald ' when the hon. gentleman was getting ready to retire. The hon. gentleman said he retired because he did not wish to run again. The Montreal ' Herald ' does not concur in that statement. It said this :
Mr. PrSfontaine was again desirous of being mayor. At the last moment he retired in favour of Mr. Wilson-Smith.
What was the result of this retirement in favour of Mr. Wilson-Smith ? I have no hesitation in saying that when he retired in favour of Mr. Wilson-Smith, he beat Mr. Wilson-Smith. That gentleman was not elected, but the man who was least expected to be elected, Mr. Cochrane, was elected mayor Of Montreal. The outside world never imagined that Mr. Cochrane would defeat Mr. Wilson-Smith; but the very fact that this hon. gentleman whose history was told in the press of the city of Montreal, retired in favour of Mr. Wilson-Smith, was quite enough to satisfy the electors with the selection of Mr. Cochrane, notwithstanding the opinion they had previously held of Mr. Wilson-Smith. If that was the stamp that was placed on his candidature, then they did not want him, and Mr. Cochrane was elected mayor. Before I sit down I should like to refer briefly to the lecture which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister saw fit to give this afternoon with regard to the differences of opinion on this side. I have been considerably at a loss to account for this lecture, because I have never before heard that any such differences of opinion existed. Of course I am only a very humble follower of my leader, but still, as we on this side have no need of Privy Council Chambers in whieh our leaders may separate themselves from their followers and do business without our counsel, we form as a whole an independant caucus of our own. where we hold counsel together, and therefore if there be anj' difficulties among us Mr. POPE.
they cannot fail to be known to every member of our party. I therefore think that I can speak with some authority on that point. Evidently some one of the right hou. gentleman's friends has been loading him up the wrong way, which, I must say, is rather cruel treatment, because he makes bad bulls-eyes enough when he does his own aiming without having his rifle loaded up and aimed for him by somebody else. He is certainly being misled, and considering that right hon. gentleman's health, it is very unfair for any of his associates to furnish him with information so utterly unfounded. I can, however, understand the right hon. gentleman's anxiety to find companions in misery, for he has certainly been rather tried of late himself. He has been compelled to part with one of his best ministers and to accept, after long hesitation, in the place of that minister, a gentleman who has been criticised by his own party press as no public man has ever before been attacked by the press of the party to which he belonged.
The hon. member for Gasp6 (Mr. Lemieux) took occasion this afternoon to inform the House that the race cry in the province of Quebec was first raised by the Conservative party. I was rather astonished to hear my hon. friend give expression to an allegation so glaringly contradicted by the facts. Sir, there was at one time in this country a gentleman who occupied the highest position among his compatriots, and who besides commanded the high esteem of this entire country. I refer to the late Sir George E. Cartier. His name has been revered by Liberal-Conservatives, from the day he first took part in politics down to the present. Was his life I ask you, Sir, a bed of roses ? Was he not rather dogged to his very grave by political organizations with which my hon. friend from Gasp 6 sympathizes ? Was he not held up to public obloquy by that very party in those days, the leaders of which to-day acknowledge him as having been the ablest champion of the French Canadian race in this country ? Sir, the same racial prejudices were then raised against him as are being raised against the leaders of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec to-day. He was accused of being too broad in his sympathies, of not being sufficiently patriotic from a narrow and sectional point of view, because liis policy was to make all races and creeds in this Dominion work in harmony. But no man to-day would say that the late Sir G. E. Cartier was not in his life time the greatest defender of the rights and interests of his compatriots which the province of Quebec ever produced. And when the hon. member for GaspS speaks of the racial cry as having been originated in the province of Quebec by the Liberal-Conservative party, I refer him to the attacks Which wero made by tbe Liberals of that day on the man whom they now recognize as having had

all the qualities of a great leader. No, Sir, it was not the Conservative party which was responsible for the exciting of the people by the racial prejudices we have heard so much of during late years. But coming down to recent days, who was the father of national prejudice in the province of Quebec of late years ? Why, everybody knows that it was the late Hon. Honors Mercier. It was he who set the province wild over racial issues. I have never heard that he was a Conservative. I have never heard that he ever had any sympathy or affiliations of any kind with the Liberal-Conservative party. And when we come down to the present day, let me say that there is no man in political life more keen than our able and our eloquent young friend from GaspS to take advantage of every small opportunity which he thinks will weigh with his own nationality. Why, I remember when, during the election in Sherbrooke, when the present member for that county (Mr. McIntosh) was opposed by Mr. T.eBaron, the cry was raised in favour of Mr. LeBaron that lie was not only a French Canadian but descended from one of the oldest families of France, and had in his veins the best French blood in the country. My hon. friend from Gaspd raised the same cry in the county of Bagot, and in fact he never fails in appealing to national Sentiment wherever and whenever he thinks such appeals can have any effect. I have always hoped, though in that hope I have been frequently disappointed, that our hen. friends opposite from the province of Quebec would, from their experience in this parliament, become seized with a broader national spirit, and when they went back again to the platform would resort to appeals of a different kind than those made this afternoon by my hon. friend from Gaspd and those around him. And I still do not despair that some day they will learn the great lesson of toleration and become convinced that it is not in the best interests of Canada nor of the French Canadian nationality in the province of Quebec to be continually trading on and prostituting what, in many respects, is one of the best sentiments of our nature.

I think, Sir, that it is of some importance that th^very words of my hon. friend, the Ministw of Marine and Fisheries, should be put on record iu the official reports of the debates of this parliament. Whether the choice which was made by the right hon. the First Minister in selecting the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the portfolio he holds, he wise or not. does not concern me at present.
The right hon. gentleman has thought fit to make the hon. gentleman one of his colleagues. It was undoubtedly his right. He has done it after a good deal of consideration, I have no doubt. I think that an hon. gentleman whom we all respect very much, the hon. Speaker of the House, had the offer of the same position, that he accepted it,
but the position did not come to him. I make that statement without divulging any secrets, for I was not in the secrets of the government then. I make the statement that the Speaker of the House got the offer of the position which the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries got later on, that he accepted it, but that-I do not know for what reason-he did not get it. That statement cannot be contradicted, because it is true. I go on quoting the words of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, so that they may be on record. It is of importance that the programme speech of an hon. gentleman who accepts a position in the government should be known, and that it should be followed, unless reasons to the contrary are given. I quote the words of the hon. gentleman to a greater extent than they have been quoted before, because it is of importance to the country at large to know how we stand in these matters. There is no doubt whatever that the hon. gentleman stated publicly, openly and solemnly that he had been authorized by his colleagues in the government to say that he would get from the Department of Public Works the control of the dredging, harbour improvements and other works relating to navigation. He made that announcement, and stated over and over again that lie had been authorized by his colleagues and by the right hon. leader of the government to make it. I shall quote the utterances of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries word for word. They were reported not only in ' La Patrie ' and ' La Presse,' but in the English papers also. There has been a campaign or discussion in the province of Quebec for about a month, especially between ' La Presse ' and ' La Patrie.' I wrote most of the articles in ' La Patrie ' to try to establish the position that the Department of Public Works should not be dismembered, while ' La Presse,' which was and still is, to a large extent, the personal organ of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, contended to the contrary, and held the view that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should have control of certain services now under the Department of Public-Works. Let me quote the very words of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I will give them first iu French :
L'accusation qui est portee contre le chef du gouvernemenfc qu'il a sacrifie la province de Qufibec en me choisissant comme un de ses col-legues et me confiant le ddpartement de la Marine et des Pficheries, est une accusation dfi-nuee de tout fondement de toutes les fagons possibles.
Comment ? on pourra le dire ailleurs, dans d'autres parties de la province oil je ne suis pas eonnu, mais on ne dira pas ici, k Montreal parmi la population qui me connait depuis vingt-cinq ans, on ne dira pas & la population de Montreal et on ne lui fera pas accroire que Raymond Prefontaine est entrd dans le cabinet Laurier en sacrifiant les interets de la province de Quebec.
II y a un autre sacrifice aussi que je n'aurais pas fait : c'est celui de nfigliger les intfirSts de

trdle et que tous les travaux qui en dependent soient aussi mis sous la mSme juridiction.
I shall not translate It into English now- it is rather long. But in two words the hon. gentleman stated then and there that he was authorized by his colleagues to say, and he spoke as a minister of the Crown-he took great care to say that he was speaking as a minister, that his word should be accepted as such-that all the harbour improvements, everything that pertained to navigation from the Yukon down, even from the north pole -he went very far-to the strait of Belle Isle, would come under his control. He made that announcement. This cannot be denied or disputed. We have been told to-day by the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that he himself in an interview had said to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that he would get something from the Department of Public Works. But my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, repeating what had been said formerly by the hon. Minister of Public Works, announced to-day, that, for the time being, the Department of Public Works would remain as it is, except that the hydrographic survey would come under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The plain facts of the case are before the country now. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries went to the electors of his own riding. He induced them to give him their suffrages. Some have been given over to companies. I intend to give these items close investigation to see whether some better arrangement cannot be devised for constructing and maintaining these works, and at another session I hope to be able to present some scheme.

The lumbering business is one of the best in the country, and the government ought not to pay money for the convenience of the lumbermen, as this is evidently for their benefit. These works ought to be self-sustaining.
Did I understand the minister to say that the government has on hand the sum of $250,000 for the purpose of building graving or dry docks ? '
If my memory serves me right, this sum is under the control of the harbour board, by Act of parliament.
These docks that are mentioned here at Levis, Kingston and Esquimau, were all built exclusively by the government ?
Yes.
Has the government come to any decision in respect to a dry dock in the vicinity of Montreal ?
No. A commission has been appointed to make a report on the best kind of dry docks, and on situations and so forth, but no decision has been come to.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell me whether there has been a report from three gentlemen appointed to make an inquiry ?
A report has been made to the department by these three gentlemen, Mr. Keating, of Toronto, and Mr. St. George and Mr. Per-rault, of Montreal.
Have these three gentlemen been appointed by Order in Council?
Yes.
Has an engineer of the Department of Public Works been engaged with these gentlemen in making that inquiry ?
Not particularly on the commission.
Have these three gentlemen been charged by my hon. friend to make an inquiry as to the choice of a site for a dry dock in Montreal ?
Speaking from memory, I think they were empowered to report on the best kinds of dry docks.

The hon. gentleman will permit me to say that neither of these three gentlemen have ever built a dry dock in his life. Mr. St. George was the municipal engineer of the city of Montreal when the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) had control of our municipal affairs. He resigned from his office after the several inquiries that took place there. He has never had any experience in building docks in his life. Mr. Maurice Perrault is an architect who has never built a dock of this kind in his life. I know Mr. Keating less. He is a very respectable man indeed, but, while he is an engineer, he has never been engaged in the construction of such works in his life. I was very much surprised when I heard that the Minister of Public Works had appointed these three men over the heads of the officers of the Public Works Department who have been engaged in building docks and other public works. We had some experience in the choice of a site in the port of Montreal. Parties tried to foist upon the harbour commission a site. There was an 941
option taken on a site for $50,000 and there was an effort made to foist a site upon the h;irbour commissioners for a quarter of a million dollars. There was a public meeting in the city of Montreal, a report of which has been published, held by the parties who wanted to make $250,000 out of the site. I am very much surprised to hear that such a commission of men, who have had no experience, has been appointed over the heads of the engineers of the Public Works Department, who have had a long experience in the construction of such works. The hon. Minister of Public Works would never have done such a thing if he had been better informed, I am sure. Mr. Maurice Perrault is a well known architect but he has never carried out any work of this kind. Mr. St. George has had no experience in that line of business. Let me say also that there is a site in one part of Montreal which the hon. Minister of Public Works will find by looking at the plans which are in his department. He will find by referring to those plans a site which will not cost a dollar to the country, a site which is alongside the shore and which is indicated on the plans of the Montreal harbour. That site is available. I speak of one site. There are other sites in other parts of the city that are also available. It is not necessary to appoint Mr. Maurice Perreault, or Mr. St. George, men who have had no experience in this line, to choose a site and much less to prepare plans. The hon. Minister of Public Works will find in his department several engineers who* have had a long experience in that kind of work. Why has he put these men over them ? We are entitled to some information on this point because this is rather a peculiar appointment that he has made. Of course, he was very new in the department; he had just taken office when the appointment was made. I call his attention to the statement I am making now and which cannot be contradicted, and it is that these two men in Montreal are architects. One of them was the municipal engineer under the late regime that the electorate of the city of Montreal got rid of during the last two municipal elections. Mr. St. George resigned after the inquiries which took place. I do not accuse him of anything. He resigned after several inquiries had taken place. Sir. Maurice Perrault is an architect in Slontreal. I want to know how it is that these men have been appointed to prepare plans and to choose a site for a dry dock in the city of Montreal when the hon. Minister of Public Works has in his own departments several engineers who have had a long experience in that kind of business.

I do not know the gentlemen in Montreal to whom the hon. member (Hon. Sir. Tarte) has referred and therefore I can say nothing about them, but when he speaks of Mr. Keating

as a man who has had no knowledge of such matters, I must tell him that he is entirely misinformed. Mr. Keating was the city engineer of Halifax, and as such superintended the construction of one of the largest dry docks on the continent of America, and he has that kind of experience which comes from the supervision of a work of that character. I do not say that he was the engineer of construction, but he was the city engineer of Halifax, and the very fact that he had gained that knowledge in the construction of one of the largest dry docks on the continent, was one of the reasons why he was chosen for this work. In respect to the other gentlemen, I cannot say anything.

The hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is mistaken in saying that these gentlemen were called upon to prepare plans for the dock. Representations were made to the government that a floating dock would be very much better for the purpose than a dry dock. A great majority of the members of the House, and I may also say, of the government are not familiar, perhaps, with the different styles of docks that are used and which are best suited to various localities. I do not know that I have a personal acquaintance with Mr. Keating, but I did ask some people from the city of Toronto as to whom they considered the best qualified engineer in that district for this purpose, and Mr. Keating's name was sent to me by a gentleman,in whom I have the greatest possible confidence. I do not think that he is a supporter of my own, nor do I know that any of the recommendations of those gentlemen came from political friends. I was anxious that we should have the benefit of the services of the most highly qualified engineers to look into this matter. They can only make report. My hon. friend said that we were ignoring the engineers in the department. That is not so. They only make a report to the chief engineer of the department and he now has it under his consideration. I have not seen it, I suppose, because he has had it under consideration, but he will report upon their recommendations before any action is taken.

It is rather strange to find two well known architects appointed on a commission to report on dry docks. I am very glad that the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) tells us that Mr. Keating has had some experience. I do not know whether he prepared the plans for the Halifax dry dock. I do not think he did, but he may have supervised the work. That does not establish in any way that the engineers of the department should have been ignored and that this matter should have been referred to men who do not belong to the civil service and are not responsible to parliament, two of them being architects,

speechtext: and one of them being the municipal engineer of the city of Montreal under the regime that has been got rid of by the municipal electors of Montreal. That is not, it seems to me, an appointment that should have been made under the circumstances. I am very anxious to see the report that these gentlemen have made. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works says that the report will be submitted to his department. Of course, it will be submitted to his department, but all the same it seems to me that this appointment is very irregular indeed. The commission is not composed of men who have had any experience in respect to dry docks.
Do I understand that these gentlemen were only appointed to visit sites in Montreal and make a report as to the most convenient site for a graving dock ?
