I have no personal knowledge of these gentlemen but they were recommended by persons in whom I had confidence.
I think the report is ready now.
My chief engineer tells me that he has it under consideration now.
Is it in the department ?
Yes.
Is there any objection to our seeing it; it is a matter of very great interest to us.
There is certainly no objection. It is a matter of public property, and I will have it brought down.

What is going to be paid to these commissioners.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS^ I think the pay was fixed not to exceed $25 a day, but my memory does not serve me as to that.
With the exception of Mr. Keating, who may perhaps have had something to do with the dry dock at Halifax-
The city of Halifax contributed to the dry dock and if he did not prepare the plans, he reported on them as city engineer.
If we have any engineer of high standing in the country, Mr. Keating is one of them.
What is the recommendation of the commissioners as to the site 1
1 have not seen the report, but I will have it brought down at the earliest possible moment.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: That is an old story. When I was minister an effort was made to foist on the Harbour Commission and on the Department of Public Works, a site for $250,000, on which an option had been taken for $50,000. Some parties tried to force that on the Harbour Commissioners. There was a public meeting held in Sohmer Park by these parties, but, of course, the effort did not succeed then. That is why I am a little careful when I discuss this item.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It may be that this is the site recommended by these Montreal engineers.
Oh, no.

As I understand it, these gentlemen were appointed to report, first, on the site, and second as to whether a floating dock or a dry dock would be best for the city of Montreal. I can bear out what my hon. friend has said : that Mr. Perrault knows no more about a floating dock or an ordinary graving dock than I do, and that is very little indeed. He is an architect of the city of Montreal ; he is a member of the Quebec legislature, but I don't think he ever saw a graving dock in his life before he went to Point Levis. As to Mr. St. George, he was simply the engineer of the city of Montreal, and in the exercise of his duties, his particular occupation was to see as to the best manner in which the city waterworks were operated. It seems strange that the government which has at its disposal men of vast experience as engineers, should go outside of the department to employ others. Of course, if they did employ men of high standing and men of experience, there would be some justification, as there is in the appointment of Mr. Keating ; but to appoint Mr. Maurice Perrault and Mr. St. George to find a site for a graving dock in the port of Montreal, and to decide as to whether a floating dock or an ordinary graving dock should be built, seems to me to be a most extraordinary proceeding on the part of the government. I do not know what is going to be the pay of these gentlemen.
The minister said it was $25 a day.

I would like to know when their pay began, and when it is going to stop ? I may tell the minister that at the last session of the Quebec legislature the Independence of Parliament Act was amended for the very purpose of allowing Mr. Perrault to accept this position from the Dominion government. This must be a permanent or a quasi permanent employment, because otherwise the legislature of Quebec would not have gone to the trouble of amending the Independence of Parliament Act to allow Mr. Perrault to help the Department of Public Works with his light in the selection of a site and in determining whether a floating or another kind of dock should be built in Montreal. I warn the Minister of Public Works that Mr. Maurice Perrault is a very high priced gentleman, and I happen to know it, because when I had the honour of being Attorney General of Quebec, the bills which he had filed with a preceding government came before me, and I may tell the minister that they were the most exorbitant bills I ever saw in my life. If he presents to this government, such a bill as he presented to the province of Quebec for work done as an architect, I am afraid the Minister of Public Works will be appalled, and he will be very sorry for ever having .employed Mr. Perrault. It seems to me, that in view of the competency of the gentlemen who are now in the Public Works Department, it is a most extraordinary thing that the government should employ two men who have no knowledge whatever and no experience whatever in such matters, and place them over the heads of their own employees. As I said before, these two gentlemen know no more about this thing than any member of the House does, and certainly they do not know as much as the engineers of the Pub-, lie Works Department.
Have negotiations been entered into for the purchase of a floating dock ? I know that there are floating docks which are very successful now.
Representations were made to the department with regard to these floating docks, but no negotiations with regard to purchase have been undertaken.

I desire to advance the work of the committee as much as possible, but this is a matter of such great interest to us that we are .justified in saying that we ought to see that report and tl;e charges of the commissioners before we pass this item. I quite agree with those who have maintained that in view of the staff which we have in the Public Works Department we did not require these commissioners at all. If it were a question of selecting a site, I think the Minister of Public Works himself, with the information he could have obtained in Montreal from gentlemen connected with the harbour, could have come

to a decision without this costly commission. As regards Mr. St. George, I am not prepared to make any condemnation of that gentleman. I have known him for many years as engineer of the city of Montreal, and I look upon him as a man of most honourable character. If it were a question of selecting a site, Mr. St. George's opinion would be valuable, but I am not aware that he has any special knowledge with regard to dry docks. I am aware, however, that he left the employment of the city for no other reason than that he desired to enter into a more profitable occupation. Mr. St. George I have known a long time ; he resides in my county, and he is a perfectly honourable man.

I think this discussion is out of order, as this vote has nothing at all to do with the matter of the committee or the building of a dry dock at Montreal. It may be interesting, politically or for some other reason, to spend a whole day in discussing these matters ; but we have done very little work, and to ask that the item stand until information is brought down on a matter with which it has nothing to do, is, I think, very unfair. I think these items ought to be considered in connection with the expenditures which they are intended to provide for. My hon. friend will have an opportunity of expressing his views with regard to the dock almost any day of the session. I know there was a great difference of opinion on the subject, and it was thought by the government that it would be a good idea to have an independent commission of expert engineers make a report upon it. One would have thought that Mr. St. George, having been for a number of years employed as an engineer by the great city of Montreal, was a man of some character and ability. However, there will be many opportunities to discuss the question of a dock ; and. as there is nothing contentious about this vote, which is the usual vote. I hope my hon. friend will not press his request that these items stand, after they have been under discussion for three or four days.

In reference to Mr. St. George, I understood one hon. gentleman to say that he was only superintendent of the water department of Montreal. I may state that he was both superintendent of the water department and city surveyor for years, at a salary of $5,300.
That would not give him any experience in graving docks.
As far as engineering is concerned. I think he is as good a man as you could get.
Even if he is a good engineer, that would not give him experience in graving docks.

I do not know what experience Mr. St. George may have had in grav-Mr. MONK.
ing docks, but my knowledge of him is that he is a perfectly honourable man. I have no objection to letting this item pass, although I do not agree with the hon. minister that this is not the place for us to ask for information on the question of a dry dock, which has been agitating public opinion for a long time. If the hon. gentleman says that he will lay that report on the Table, at the earliest opportunity, I have no objection to letting the item pass.
Certainly ; it will be brought down as soon as the engineer makes his report.
I would like very much to know whether the crane for the L6vis dock which we were talking about when I left office has been placed ?
Not yet.
Is the work under contract or under way ?
No, it is not under way. I will inquire into that. It has never been brought to my attention.

I understand that this commission of three gentlemen was appointed to investigate the question of a dry dock or select a site. Now that their report is in, I suppose their duties are ended, and their services have been dispensed with ?

Yes.
Telegraph lines-Prince Edward Island and mainland, $2,000.
This $2,000 is voted under an arrangement made at the time of confederation for maintaining the telegraph line with Prince Edward Island.

I would like to ask the minister if he or the government has received any communication from the provincial government, requesting this amount to be withheld, until the Anglo-American Telegraph Company fulfil their contract to give us an up-to-date service ?

No, I have no such communication. I was visited by a deputation, representing, I think, the board of trade, asking me to make some effort to have better telegraphic facilities with the island, better rates, and longer hours. The matter is now receiving the consideration of the department.
I would like to ask the minister if it is not in the power of this government to withhold this amount while the company neglect to give us the service they should ?

I would not like to offer an opinion off-

band on that point. It is a question on which even the best lawyers might differ. However, the matter is now receiving the consideration of the department, in view of the application made for better rates.
Land and cable telegraph lines, lower St. Lawrence and maritime provinces, including working expenses of vessels required for cable service, also maintenance of Marconi wireless telegraphy at Belle Isle, $80,000.
Would the bon. minister tell us how the Marconi stations which have been installed, one at Belle Isle and one on the north shore, have been working during the last few months ?
I have not myself given the matter much personal attention, but my information from the officers of my department is that latterly they have been working remarkably well.

I would, invite my hon. friend's personal attention to these two stations. 1 was informed by some of the officers that they were working splendidly, and I began sending dispatches myself and asking for reports every day, but the reports did not materialize very quickly. I say that some of the officers are very fine men indeed, but they take for granted that the Marconi system is working splendidly when it does not work at all. My hon. friend will find in the department a record of the telegrams which I sent asking for an answer, which did not come quickly. I think the House will agree with me that it is very important to know exactly how this Marconi system works. Every time there is some stock to be placed on the market, it works splendidly, but when the stock is placed, it does not work so well. I would like very much to know how these two stations work. Will my hon. friend be good enough to inquire how many days the two stations have been working. Occasionally on a dry day one of the stations would work, and the next day, although also a dry day, it would not work at all. Then on a damp day it would work splendidly, and on the following day, which was also damp, it would refuse to work.

I think the matter is one of very great importance, not because of the small service we have, but for the experience this will give the country. I have not been able to give it personal attention, but I am informed that for a long time it was very unsatisfactory, tout that latterly it is giving satisfaction. Iam asking for a detailed report of all imformation regarding the working of the system and will have that laid on the Table.
Are all the cables in working order now, between the North Shore and Belle Isle, for instance ?

The cable at the Grosse Isle Quarantine
station is out of order. We had a report recently that there is something wrong with the cable at Anticosti, but that is now being attended to.
Is the cable at Belle Isle in full working order ?
It is.

I know that for several seasons this cable has been out of order. I had occasion to write my hon. friend when he was Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), complaining that it was very seldom during the summer season that one could get a telegram to Point Aux Esquimaux. I had occasion to cable to Point Aux Esquimaux several times, and my dispatches were not received. It appears that there is a bay there, and the cable between the two points separated by this bay is almost always out of order, and the way dispatches are sent is to give the dispatch at one point to a schooner which takes it to the other point, some six or seven miles or more distant. This is not a quick method of sending telegrams. If the tide happens to be out or the wind is not right, you do not get your telegram delivered for five or six days.
My hon. friend is speaking of the cable on the North Shore off Anticosti as being out of order.

I do not say that it is now out of order, but am calling attention to the fact that it is too often out of order especially during the season of navigation. I wrote the ex-Minister of Public Works on the subject, as he will remember. I do not know what is the cause, but would ask my hon. friend to look into it. Some years ago the ' Scotsman ' was wrecked off Belle Isle, and for want of communication between the mainland and Belle Isle the passengers on the ' Scotsman ' could not get succour from the mainland. They were three or four-days without relief simply because there was no cable communication. Now that you have the Marconi system, the object for which it was established is to give assistance in cases such as I have just mentioned and also to give information at Quebec aud other ports as to the state of navigation in these straits-for instance as to whether there are icebergs in the stra'its and any other information affecting navigation. It is of the greatest importance not only that the cable of the mainland should be kept in perfect working order during the season of navigation, but that these Marconi stations should be so kept up that they will be of service to the country and navigation.

I understand that they had a good deal of difficulty with the cable itself to which my hon. friend refers, but that latterly it is

working first rate. I am asking for all information and will have a report made.
Is Mr. Boyer still tlie chief officer in charge of the lines in the lower St. Lawrence 1
Yes.
He is a good official, indeed, and I am glad that he has been kept on.
Does this amount represent the whole amount paid Mr. Marconi ?

We pay no royalty., All we purchased we paid for. My understanding is that on account of the grant we 'have given, we get the instruments without paying any royalty, and the small amount referred to here is for the maintenance of the two instruments established there. That will cover the salaries of two men and any small repairs there may be. My deputy informs me that the estimate made for the maintenance of this service is $4,200, and I am asking for detailed information with regard to the daily work of these stations. That report ought to be down within the next week, as I do not see why there should be any particular delay.
Might'I ask if this item, as well as the other we passed this evening, are in any danger of 15eing transferred to the Marine Department.
Oh, we have had enqugh of that.
I intend to spend this money if allowed to do it.

I was absent for a time, and did not hear the discussion, but perhaps, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) would give us an idea whether, so far, the Marconi system has worked so satisfactorily as to give evidence of being useful.

We have had quite a discussion in the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Osier's) absence. I am only too pleased to be able to tell him that the officers of the department consider that latterly the system has been working satisfactorily. What I have engaged to do-and I think it is of public importance to get the information-is to get a statement in detail showing the working of the Marconi system at Belle Isle.
Telegraph lines-North-west Territory, $20,-
000.
How far does the hon. minister propose to go to-night ?

I have been sitting here from three o'clock this afternoon, and it would be very proper for me to say that we took up a lot of time Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
in discussing a matter not at all so important as the voting of these supplies. This is the third or fourth day we have been trying to get a discussion of these items. I think that this item, No. 238, ought to pass tonight.
I suppose there will be something in the supplementary estimates in regard to the Yukon line ?

I have said so. I may say to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that I do not know of any item here the substance of which will not come up at an early day in case any body may wish to discuss them.
That is very good. Sometimes, the supplementary estimates have not come down at an early day. But my hon. friend says that they will

I will give an undertaking that they will be down at an early day.
Telegraph lines-British Columbia, $15,000.
What is this for ?

This vote is the same as last year. It is for the maintenance of these lines in British Columbia, the payment of salaries and small repairs. I have details here as to where the lines are located, the distances, &e., hut my hon. friend (Sir. Ingram), of course, is familiar with them, and would not wish me to give details to-night.
Where do we find the statement of the receipts of these lines ?

In the Auditor General's Report.
Telegraph lines-Yukon Territory (Ashcroft-Dawson line and branches), $121,000.

May I ask the hon. minister if he is in a position to tell us the receipts and expenditures on the Yukon lines ? If he has not the information at hand, I will wait until the supplementary estimates are before us. Is Mr. Crean still in charge of these lines ?
Yes.
Has he still Mr. Rochester with him ?
Yes.
Who is really in charge, Mr. Rochester or Mr. Crean ?
Mr. Crean.
Mr. Crean has more authority than Mr. Rochester V

Well, he is the superintendent. Mr. Rochester, I understand, is sent out to look after the accounts and straighten matters up. The hon. leader of the opposition has asked me to state the receipts and expenditures of last year. In round numbers the receipts were $111,000, and the expenditures $179,000.
Has there been any lowering of the rates 1
Yes, the rates were lowered from $4.50 to $3.
When ?
Last July.

I would ask my hon. friend to bring down, as soon as he can, the details of the expenditure. I am somewhat in doubt as to the figures that have been mentioned. I know the hon. gentleman will give his best attention to that item, because when I left office there was some little difficulty that was not settled. I will take it very kindly if he will bring down the details of expenditure as soon as he can-that is to say, before we vote more money for this line, so that the House may know exactly where we stand. I generally had a statement every month, showing the income and expenditure, and I am appalled at the deficit which we have to face.

I am afraid, if my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) left some little difficulties existing when he left office, I found some little difficulties existing when I took office. I have been inquiring, and trying to find out how the matter stands ever since. We shall have to ask a supplementary vote, and we can have the matter further discussed. I gave instructions to have a full detailed report with regard to this matter, and I expect to have it ready next week.

I would suggest that this item be allowed to stand over. The sum is an enormous one. During the first year of operating a telegraph in the Yukon, one can understand that the expenses would be heavy, but they might be expected to decrease after the line is in reasonably good order. This sum seems to be so large for the service, that I think we should have the fullest details of the expenditure before the item passes.

I quite agree with that proposition, but I do not see any advantage in allowing this matter to stand. As I have already said, we have to ask for a supplementary vote, and I have promised to bring down the fullest detailed report, which I have ordered to be made some time ago, and which I am informed will be ready next week. There will be another item on which we can discuss the whole matter.

Can we expect that Mr. Rochester will be back before the end of the session ? I have confluence in his judgment and in his hondur, and I would like to have him here, if he can be spared from his present post. When I left office I had instructed him to go up there and settle some little difficulties we had. I gave him full authority to take charge of the books and the whole business. I think my letter will be found in the Department of Public Works. I want Mr. Rochester's report.

Mr. Rochester is up there carrying out the instructions given him by the minister. There has been no change in his instructions, except that the deputy minister may have informed him that I wanted the matter settled and the fullest details obtained. With regard to the presence of Mr. Rochester here, I may say that when my hon. friend who was at the head of the department gets Mr. Rochester's report, if he is not satisfied with it, then he can get Mr. Rochester to come down. He may be back within the next few weeks, and we can call him back at any time. At present I think he is at White Horse.
I notice that the revenue for the month of April, 1902, on the Yukon telegraph line, was $11,500. How does that compare with last year ?
We have not yet a return for the present year.
In a general way, is the revenue increasing on the Yukon telegraph line ?
Since the decrease in the rates in July last, I am afraid there has been a general decrease in the receipts. The increased business lias not been sufficient to make up for the reduced rate.
Perhaps the minister has before him the revenue for some one month during last year ?

In 1902 the receipts, in round numbers, were, for July, $12,000; August, $12,000 ; September, $14,000; October, $12,000, November, $7,900; December, $4,733. We can only estimate the receipts since January as we have not the returns.
Did you get the returns of these receipts by mail or by telegraph ?
The deputy informs me that they are telegraphed at the end of each month. The last return we have is for February or March.

It would seem that we are running that line at a loss of $89,090,

and still we are told there will be another item in the supplementary estimates in addition. Evidently we are running it at a great loss. We were led to expect that after the line was completed there would he a reduction in the expenses of operation, but we have here for the staff $100,000, and it seems that won't toe enough, because we are told there will be another item in the supplementaries for that purpose. We ought to get full information of the revenue and of the expenditures, and we ought to ascertain why the expenditure continues to be so high.

I have already explained to the committee that this item will have to be increased by some $50,000 or $00,000. I agree that the committee is entitled to the fullest information, and I am desirous of obtaining this information for the committee and for the department, so that we may know whether there is any prospect of reducing the expenditure.
What is the length of the line ?
In round figures, about 2,000 miles.
How did that line work during the winter months ? Were there many breakages ?
There were quite a number of accidents through storms and trees falling, and for some days there was no service. But under the circumstances the service is fairly good.

I cannot understand why there is such a large deficit. During the last six months before I left office the revenue was a little over the expenditure, we had a little surplus every month. I am afraid there must toe something wrong in tiie way the accounts have been prepared, because I do not see how we can be running behind so much. Generally we have a balance on the right side.

I am afraid my hon. friend must have been misled by the reports be was receiving. But as I say, we cannot discuss this matter intelligently until we have a full statement of the accounts before us, and this we will have in a short time.

I think this item :s altogether too large to pass. As .he minister has nor the information, I do not think we should pass it. I do not think we can pass blindly $121,000 on the promise of the minister that the matter will be discussed cn the supplementary estimates.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend. If after full investigation of the accounts of the present year it Is shown that this $121,-Mr. SPROULE.
000	will be sufficient, everybody would be very well pleased. I have given the committee the information which, probably if
1	had wanted to get this vote through I might have withheld. I have said that, basing it upon the estimate of last year, it will require $58,000 in round numbers, and that before a vote was asked for in the supplementary estimates we would have a full return in regard to the expenses and operation of the line and all the accounts explained and that we would then ask only what was necessary.
How is this estimate of $121,000 made up ?
This is for salaries and expenses in connection with the operation of the line.
Give us the details then 1
I think it is very unreasonable at this hour of the night to ask me to go through this long list of names, but I will do it if the hon. gentleman insists.
It seems to me that on an item of $121,000 we should have more information, especially when the hon. minister acknowledged that he has not the Information to give to the committee.
I never made any such statement.

I beg pardon, because I understand that is what the hon. gentleman said. He said that he could not give the information as to the expenditures and how they were incurred until he had further information, and that he hoped later on when the supplementary estimates came down that he would be able to give that information. This is altogether too large an item to pass without having full information upon it.

The hon. gentleman is altogether mistaken. The accounts that my hon. friend is referring to I have given in detail and it is quite a different thing from the matter of voting money for the maintenance and operation of the line. The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was asking for the full accounts in connection with the expenditure for the current year. That is quite a different thing.
I am asking for the particulars of the expenditure under the estimates.
If my hon. friend insists upon it I will have to read this list. But he will see how unreasonable his request is in view of the ten or twelve hour sitting we have had.
Nothing is unreasonable when you are asking for information.

No, certainly not, when you are asking for information, but I will leave it to the committee if in connection with any item that has ever been presented in the history of parliament it is usual to require a minister to stand up and read page after page of the names of employees with the monthly pay they are receiving and to give every detail to show how the estimate is made up.

It is quite within
the right of any one to ask for that information, but at the same time there is no desire to take up time unduly. Would it not be better to let the hon. Minister of Public Works hand the statement to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) and then we probably could dispose of these items in a few minutes at the next sitting of the House ?
Yes, I only want to get the information as to how this expenditure is made up.

My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) has not been here for days and days, and weeks and weeks, during which we have been sitting night after night. We are most anxious to get on with the business of the House. If he would make any reasonable proposition I would be only too delighted to comply with his request.

In your position surely you must expect to be called upon to do some work and you must not grumble if it takes you some time to get through with your estimates. All I want to know is what this expenditure is for. Is it for salaries, or for maintenance ? This is not an item that we can be reasonably asked to pass without full information.
Perhaps the hon. minister would be in a position to tell us what is the monthly expenditure for the working of the Dawson line ?
The estimate of the expenditure for next year for salaries, as it has been made up, is $123,885.12. I have detailed information showing every man's name, his occupation, and the amount of his salary.
How many officers are there in this service ?
About 125.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us what was the expenditure, say, for the month of March ? We used to have a report every month of the expenditure and revenue.
The report has not reached the department yet as to the expenditure.
Has there been a telegraphic report for February ?
The average salaries would perhaps be about $11,000 per month.
We thought it would be about that much when I left office. Again I say I cannot understand why we have such a deficit.

Unless the salaries alone can be reduced very much next year I do not think there should be any objection to granting this present estimate now of $121,000 because I have explained to the committee that unless the expenditure can be materially reduced for the coming year we will have to ask for a supplementary vote. The ex-Minister of Public Works said that he had sent a man out there in whom he had every confidence to make a full inquiry and report. I have no reason to doubt either the honesty or the qualifications of the gentleman he sent there to make this report, and when we get it we will have the officers of the department make a detailed statement of everything in connection with the expenditure as to the building of the line and as to the operation of it during the past year. Then the hon. member for West Toronto (Ml-. Osier) as well as other hon. gentlemen can exercise their judgment as to whether any reduction can be made in future or any change in the rates charged.

I cannot understand how it is that we have lost such a large amount of money on that line. During the last six months before I left office the expenditure and the revenue were about equal. We had some little balance in our favour and I cannot understand how we made a loss of $70,000 a year. I am very much afraid that the accounts have been prepared by somebody in such a way as to charge to working expenses sums of money that should have been charged to some other account.
Is there an office every sixteen miles ?
There is a house of refuge every sixteen miles and the offices are about thirty miles apart.
I hope I have made myself properly understood. I instructed Mr. Rochester to take charge of the whole organization and I hope my instructions have been followed.

So far as I am concerned no change has been made in the instructions given. Nothing has been brought to my attention to create any doubt as to his qualifications and good intentions, and whatever instructions were given, if he has carried them out faithfully, are the instructions he is working under.
Has Mr. Rochester made any report as yet ?
He is in communication with the deputy from time to time, but his report as to the full statement has not come yet.

I am quite sure that such a deficit as has been mentioned is not the genuine deficit of last year. I knew the circumstances before I left office, and unless there has been some accident and something charged to the working expenses which might be charged in some other way, I think the line is about self-sustaining.
We will get all that information.

When a minister comes to ask for such a vote as this, he ought to be prepared to give us information and not -ask us to vote $123,000 blind. We have had difficulty in getting information about this on previous occasions and every succeeding year the difficulty seems to be getting worse.

I have given the estimate made by the officers of the department, and I have the details here as to the salaries and the persons who receive them. The estimate is based on the expenditure of last year and that is the only way an estimate can be made. I do not know what the hon. gentleman refers to when he says he did not get satisfactory information in the past. I have all the information on which this estimate is based, but we are speaking of a separate matter, namely, tlie details for the current year.
My complaint is that this is all estimate without any intelligent data being given.
It is based upon the actual expenditure of past years as contained in the books of the department.
And if we ask for this information later on we may he met with the reply that it is not to hand.

I do not think that is a fair statement to make. These people have to be paid monthly, and I am sorry to say that as the appropriation has been overdrawn, they have not received their pay for some time. What we have been speaking about is the detailed accounts which have not yet come in.

We should know the cost of operating the line and the cost of keeping it in repair. I do not think that there is any necessity for an office every sixteen miles in such a country as that, and that is perhaps the reason why there is a deficit.
I have all the information here, but it would take a long time to read it, and I would be pleased if my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) would permit me to hand him a copy.
The minister will send a copy to my hon. friend (Mr. Osier).

I shall be pleased indeed.
Some resolutions reported.

Ill moving the adjournment of the House, permit me to call attention to a telegram which I have received, and which will be very gratifying to members on both sides. The flag was placed at half-mast to-day, not only because of the funeral of the late Mr. Justice Mills, but also because the announcement was made of the death of Senator Cochrane, of Hillhurst, Que. A telegram has been placed in my hand from a member of Mr. Cochrane's family contradicting the report of his death, and stating that the hon. gentleman is much better.
What business does the hon. gentleman expect to take up to-morrow ?
There are several notices of motion and resolutions in committee which will be taken up first, and after that Supply. The Minister of Justice will proceed with his estimates.
There are two or three items under Public Works which were allowed to stand, and they might be cleaned up.
We will proceed, then, with the Public Works' estimates first, and after that, if the Minister of Justice is present, we will take his estimates.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Thursday, May 14, 1903.
